item.title: Swiss pensions: go-ahead for substitute taxation
item.description: QuotidianoPiù announces the go-ahead for the substitute tax on Swiss pensions.
item.content:encoded:
## TL;DR - The topic is substitute taxation. - The measure concerns Swiss pensions. - The headline refers to approval.
## Key facts - Swiss → pensions theme - Substitute → taxation measure - Outcome → clear
The title published by QuotidianoPiù announces the green light to substitute taxation for Swiss pensions. This is the verifiable core of the news available: a green light referring to the tax treatment of Swiss annuities, without further elements in the material provided.
### What is confirmed The wording does not indicate which authority has given the green light, which act contains it, from when the measure starts or which pensioners are affected. It also does not present amounts, rates, thresholds or a comparison between periods. For this reason, the announcement can be reported for what it says, that is, a green light to substitute taxation, but not transformed into an operational sheet.
The distinction is relevant for those who live or work in Switzerland and receive an income: the title identifies the subject, not the details needed to calculate the tax. Any reference to AVS/AHV or LPP/BVG is also not specified in the available source. The text, therefore, does not allow to attribute the novelty to a specific component of Swiss social security. ## How to read the tax profile
The verified overview of Swiss taxation helps establish the scope of the news item, without adding details not contained in the headline. Taxation is structured at three levels: direct federal tax, cantonal tax and municipal tax. Each canton has its own law and multiplier; for municipalities, the multiplier is applied to the cantonal tax.
### The three levels of taxation | Level | Verified element | |---|---| | Federal | Direct federal tax | | Cantonal | The canton’s own law and multiplier | | Municipal | Multiplier applied to the cantonal tax |
The news item about the approval does not say which of these levels the substitute taxation refers to. It is therefore not possible to establish, based on the headline alone, whether the effect concerns IFD, cantonal taxation, municipal taxation or a combination of the levels. This is the concrete comparison the data allow: the tax system comprises three levels, while the available source identifies only its general subject.
The distinction also applies with respect to social security. In the verified facts, UFAS/BSV is the social security office, with reference to AVS/AI/LPP, and does not set taxes. Therefore, the role of UFAS/BSV cannot be used to attribute the approval announced by QuotidianoPiù to that body. ## What remains to be verified
The headline does not document the effective date of the measure, the statutory text, the taxable base, any substitute tax rate or the scope of the pensions involved. Nor does it provide an amount to compare with direct federal tax or with cantonal and municipal levies. These elements cannot be inferred from the mere reference to Swiss pensions.
For the social security aspect, the [AVS 2026 summary table](https://www.ahv-iv.ch/p/2.01.i) is the official reference identified in the available materials for AVS, AI and IPG. The reference serves to keep social security data separate from the tax news item: the table does not document the substitute taxation announced in the headline. The same criterion applies to UFAS/BSV: its remit is social security, not the setting of tax rates.
The approval therefore remains the central fact, while scope, timeline and calculation remain outside the verifiable scope. The headline does not even make it possible to establish whether AVS/AHV pensions, LPP/BVG benefits or another category are involved. To follow the social security topic without confusing pensions and taxes, consult calcolatore AVS/LPP/rendita.
*Source: [quotidianopiu.it](https://www.quotidianopiu.it/dettaglio/10919028/pensioni-svizzere-via-libera-allimposizione-sostitutiva)*

item.title: ETERIA: Berta Serret launches Smart Luxury brand with lab-grown diamonds and recycled gold
item.description: On November 11, 2026, Berta Serret officially launches ETERIA JEWELLERY online: sustainable fine jewelry blending IGI-certified lab-grown diamonds
item.content:encoded:
## TL;DR - European online launch on November 11, 2026 for ETERIA, founded by Berta Serret - "Smart Luxury" positioning bridging traditional fine jewelry and accessible luxury - Exclusively crafted with CoC-certified recycled gold and IGI-certified lab-grown diamonds - 100% individual piece traceability provided through TRACEMARK
## Key facts - Launch date → November 11, 2026 - Founder → Berta Serret (second generation Facet Barcelona, founder of Tracemark) - Core concept → Smart Luxury (noble materials, ethical transparency, competitive pricing) - Materials → 18K, 14K, and 9K recycled gold (CoC certified); IGI-certified lab-grown diamonds - Entry bestseller → 18K gold solitaire ring with 1ct lab-grown diamond at €999 - Debut collection → The Classics Edition - Official store → [eteriajewellery.com](https://eteriajewellery.com/)
November 11, 2026 marks the official European online launch of ETERIA JEWELLERY, the new contemporary fine jewelry brand founded by entrepreneur Berta Serret. Deeply rooted in the international jewelry industry, Serret represents the second generation of the family behind Facet Barcelona and six years ago established TRACEMARK, the pioneering consortium for certified end-to-end traceability in jewelry. With ETERIA, she introduces her most personal entrepreneurial venture, uniting traditional jewelry technical mastery with a forward-looking, sustainable vision under the banner of "Smart Luxury".
Having grown up immersed in the jewelry world—accompanying her father on business travels and attending premier international fairs like Baselworld in Switzerland and Vicenzaoro since age 14—Serret recognized an unaddressed gap in the European and Swiss markets: the void between heritage fine jewelry with steep price barriers and fleeting costume jewelry.
ETERIA fills this space with a balanced philosophy: creating refined pieces from noble materials designed to be worn effortlessly from day to evening, upholding uncompromising craftsmanship and sustainability at competitive direct-to-consumer prices. ## The Smart Luxury framework: recycled gold, lab-grown diamonds, and traceability
ETERIA's business model rests on three distinct standards: independent gemological certification, audited recycled gold, and individual piece traceability. The brand exclusively utilizes lab-grown diamonds certified by the International Gemological Institute (IGI) paired with recycled gold bearing Chain of Custody (CoC) certification. Furthermore, each jewel includes a dedicated digital traceability passport powered by TRACEMARK, mapping every step from raw metal sourcing and casting to stone cutting and setting.
This integrated approach delivers unprecedented accessibility without compromising luxury standards. The brand's signature entry piece—an 18K gold solitaire ring featuring a 1-carat IGI-certified lab-grown diamond with verified TRACEMARK traceability—is offered at €999, redefining the benchmark for classic fine jewelry.
| Feature | Conventional Fine Jewelry | ETERIA Model (Smart Luxury) | |---|---|---| | Diamond sourcing | Mined diamonds | IGI-certified lab-grown diamonds | | Gold origin | Standard mined or mixed gold | 100% CoC-certified recycled gold | | Piece traceability | Rarely available per item | 100% individual TRACEMARK passport | | Customization | Bespoke or catalog-restricted | Interactive "Design your Own" configuration | | Value proposition | High multi-tier retail markups | Direct-to-consumer accessibility (€999 for 1ct solitaire) |
### Bespoke personalization through "Design your Own"
A central feature of the customer experience is the "Design your Own" module, enabling customers to tailor each creation to their exact preferences. Shoppers can choose gold purity (18K, 14K, or 9K), gold hue (classic yellow gold or sleek white gold), as well as diamond cut (round brilliant, pear, oval, or emerald) and carat weight.
This bespoke capability gives wearers the freedom to match design and budget seamlessly. To explore customization options and purchase directly online across Europe and Switzerland, visit the official store at [eteriajewellery.com](https://eteriajewellery.com/). ## From the debut collection to Swiss and European expansion
ETERIA begins its market journey with *The Classics Edition*, a collection honoring timeless jewelry staples including four-prong solitaires, halo rings, and delicate pavé settings. Forthcoming lines will expand the catalog into *The Tennis Edition* and *The High Jewellery Edition*.
Ahead of today's official e-commerce rollout on November 11, 2026, the preliminary European pre-sale achieved robust momentum. Over its initial four weeks, the brand established partnerships with 50 physical retail points of sale across Europe and recorded over €250,000 in early wholesale revenue.
The direct-to-consumer digital channel launched today forms the cornerstone of ETERIA's growth strategy, designed to complement its expanding retail network throughout Europe and Switzerland. In a Swiss market deeply attuned to watchmaking mastery, fine craftsmanship, and ethical sustainability, Berta Serret's venture provides a modern, transparent luxury choice: noble, verifiable, and designed to endure.
To discover the collections and shop online, visit the official website at [eteriajewellery.com](https://eteriajewellery.com/).

item.title: 3 in 10 businesses delay or cut investments: red tape
item.description: According to the RG 12.30 service of November 9, 2026, for three out of ten Swiss companies, administrative constraints result in the postponement
item.content:encoded:
## TL;DR - Three out of ten businesses postpone, reduce or cancel investments - 67% consider the administrative burden high - 64% report more bureaucracy over the last five years
## Key facts - Date → November 9, 2026 - Research → gfs.bern for economiesuisse - Sample → 1’527 companies interviewed - High administrative burden → 67% - Bureaucracy on the rise → 64% over the last five years
According to the RG 12.30 report of November 9, 2026, for three out of ten Swiss companies, administrative constraints lead to the postponement, reduction or cancellation of investments. The percentage emerged from a national study conducted by gfs.bern on behalf of economiesuisse and published on the same day.
The survey quantifies the burden and describes some of its effects. 67% of the 1’527 companies interviewed consider it high. 64% also report an increase in bureaucracy over the last five years. The description of the difficulties includes complex procedures and duplicate requests from the authorities.
The limitations identified by the study particularly affect two areas: the development of new products and services and the training of apprentices. The source does not measure these effects with a separate percentage, but lists them among the activities affected by administrative constraints.
### economiesuisse's position
This position was expressed during a joint press conference. Silvan Wildhaber, president of economiesuisse, described the growing burden as “a problem made at home” that needs to be corrected to preserve jobs and prosperity, according to the written version of his statement.
The statement differs from the numerical results: 67% and 64% are findings from the study, while Wildhaber's wording is a position expressed by the association's president. The text therefore reports both a measurement of companies' responses and the call to correct the administrative burden, without indicating that a reform has already been adopted. ## How to read the three measures
The three central figures in the research do not measure the same question. The share of three out of ten businesses concerns a concrete investment decision: postponement, reduction or cancellation. The 67% instead measures the assessment of the administrative burden, while the 64% concerns the perception of an increase in bureaucracy over the last five years. Expressed as a percentage, the fraction of three out of ten corresponds to 30%; the numerical comparison between 67 and 64 shows a difference of three percentage points. The meaning, however, remains different: one percentage describes the burden judged high, the other a change perceived over time.
| Indicator | What it represents in the source | |---|---| | Three out of ten businesses | Investments postponed, reduced or cancelled | | 67% of 1’527 companies | Administrative burden judged high | | 64% | Bureaucracy increased over the last five years |
The source does not present a cross-tabulation of these responses. It therefore does not make it possible to establish how many companies have simultaneously judged the burden to be high, reported an increase over the last five years, and modified their investments. The reference period is also not identical: five years are indicated for the growth in bureaucracy, while no interval is specified for investment decisions.
### From measurement to requests
The transition from the results to the proposals is explicit in the text of the economic associations. To ease the pressure, the business community calls for the complete digitalization of processes: one-stop shops, standardized forms and transmission of data only once to all levels of government. The request for one-time transmission is directly linked to the complaint about duplicate requests; it does not, however, demonstrate that such a solution has already been introduced.
The associations also call for a substantial streamlining of regulation. In explaining this request, they recall that more than 36’000 obligations apply to companies at the federal level. The proposed direction is a risk-based regulatory approach, rather than one based on detailed prescriptions. The package is rounded out by the removal of technical barriers to trade and support for strategic agreements such as Bilaterals III.
The comparison thus separates evidence, interpretation and proposal: the survey quantifies perceptions and curtailed investments; the associations identify administrative and regulatory tools to ease the pressure. The source does not provide a measured result after these tools have been applied. ## From results to sector positions
The service supplements the survey results with the concerns of leaders from various economic sectors. Their statements do not provide new percentages, but highlight specific obstacles facing their respective sectors.
Annette Luther, president of scienceindustries, emphasizes that chemical-pharmaceutical innovation requires rapid approval procedures. Martin Hirzel, president of Swissmem, instead denounces declining margins and rising regulatory costs in the technology sector. Stefan Mäder, president of the Swiss Insurance Association, argues that the competitiveness of the economic hub should be considered an explicit regulatory objective.
### Three different emphases
The three statements distinguish three points of focus: approval times for chemical-pharmaceutical innovation, the relationship between margins and regulatory costs in technology, and recognition of competitiveness as a regulatory objective. These are positions attributed to the presidents of the associations mentioned, not a new statistical survey separate from the national survey.
The text does not break down the results by company size, area or individual economic sector, nor does it indicate which authorities formulated the duplicate requests complained about by businesses. Nor does it provide a timetable for digitization, regulatory streamlining or the elimination of technical barriers to trade. Bilateral III is listed among the agreements to be supported, without the source reporting an outcome already achieved.
Even the objective of preserving jobs and well-being, referred to by Wildhaber, is not accompanied by a quantification of jobs lost or safeguarded. The documented conclusion therefore remains limited: the research points to a high administrative burden, an increase perceived over the last five years, and investments postponed, reduced or cancelled; the associations add requests for simplification and digitization to these data. To explore the employment side of the issue, see job listings.
*Source: [rsi.ch](https://www.rsi.ch/s/4227656)*

item.title: Pamini (Udc): wages and cross-border workers, act through contributions
item.description: The editorial headline presents Pamini (Udc) with a precise indication: link the issue of wages and cross-border commuters to the chapter
item.content:encoded:
## TL;DR - Pamini links salaries, cross-border commuters and contributions - AVS/AI/IPG: 5.3% borne by the employee - LPP: rates from 7% to 18% by age bracket - LAMal: per-capita premium, not a salary contribution
## Key facts - Position → act with contributions - AVS/AI/IPG → 5.3% employee; 10.6% total - AD/AC → 1.1% up to the annual ceiling - LAINF/LAA → 0.7–1.5% by industry - LPP → 7%, 10%, 15% and 18% on the coordinated salary - LAMal → mandatory for residents
The editorial title presents Pamini (UdC) with a precise indication: connect the issue of salaries and border workers to the chapter on contributions. However, the wording does not indicate a new rate, a change in the law, an effective date or an amount. To remain adherent to the source, the analysis therefore starts from the items defined in the Swiss framework and does not attribute further measures to Pamini.
For salary, the first distinction concerns AVS/AI/IPG. The share indicated to be borne by the employee is 5.3%; with the employer, the overall total indicated is 10.6%. AD/AC unemployment is indicated at 1.1% up to an annual ceiling. For LAINF/LAA accident insurance, the range is 0.7–1.5% and varies by industry. These are percentages: without the reference salary, the period and ceiling in francs do not produce a net monthly income on their own.
### The items that the title brings to the center
The LPP/BVG follows a specific reference: the coordinated salary. The grid provided indicates 7% between 25 and 34 years, 10% between 35 and 44, 15% between 45 and 54 and 18% from 55 years up to the reference age. The sequence shows that age is a mechanism variable. However, it does not authorise the percentages to be converted into an individual amount, because the material does not show a coordinated salary, month of pay or detailed distribution of the individual envelope.
The LAMal/KVG premium must be kept separate from salary deductions. Health insurance is mandatory for residents and must be taken out within three months of arrival. The premium is private and per capita: it is not a tax and it is not a salary contribution. For adults, the deductibles indicated are CHF 300, 500, 1000, 1500, 2000 and 2500. Premiums depend on canton and region, while premium reduction is a cantonal subsidy. The link with the cost of living exists at the level of monthly expenditure, but does not change the nature of the item.
The reference to frontiersmen requires the same caution. The title does not specify whether the desired action concerns AVS/AI/IPG, unemployment, accidents, LPP or another component, nor does it indicate an audience, an amount or a calendar. The verifiable data is the theme: reading wages and cross-border work through contributions. The rest must be kept separate from the rules already defined for residents, employees and policyholders. Thus the phrase attributed to Pamini remains an editorial orientation, it does not become a reform that the source does not describe. ## Contributions, taxes and premiums on three levels
The relevant comparison is not between isolated percentages, but between different bases. An item may be calculated on salary, tied to a cap, adjusted according to sector or age, or set as a per-capita premium. Putting everything under the word contributions creates a misleading comparison.
The first level concerns deductions linked to employment. AVS/AI/IPG, AD/AC, LAINF/LAA and LPP/BVG are presented with different mechanisms. The first three items are expressed within the framework of salary contributions; LPP, by contrast, uses the coordinated salary and an age-bracket scale. LAMal/KVG does not belong to this same base, because the premium is per capita and does not depend on a percentage of salary.
| Item | Mechanism | Verified data | |---|---|---| | AVS/AI/IPG | Percentage of salary | 5.3% employee; 10.6% total | | AD/AC | Percentage up to an annual cap | 1.1% | | LAINF/LAA | Rate according to sector | 0.7–1.5% | | LPP/BVG | Coordinated salary and age bracket | 7%, 10%, 15%, 18% | | LAMal/KVG | Per-capita premium for residents | Not a salary contribution |
The second level is fiscal. Switzerland provides for three levels: direct federal tax, cantonal tax and municipal tax. Each Canton has its own law and multiplier. The municipality applies a multiplier to the cantonal tax. A figure for the AVS/AHV percentage, therefore, does not replace the calculation of direct federal tax or that of cantonal and municipal taxes.
### Institutional responsibilities
The offices also have distinct areas of responsibility. AFC/ESTV is responsible for direct federal tax and VAT. Cantonal administrations manage the cantonal and municipal levels. UFAS/BSV concerns social security, including AVS, AI and LPP, but does not set taxes. UST/BFS produces statistics and does not establish tax rates. This separation prevents assigning to one body a decision that belongs to another level.
For someone reading a Swiss payslip, the distinction is concrete: a contribution deduction, an insurance premium and a tax burden are not interchangeable. The same applies to the cost of living. A LAMal premium may affect monthly expenses, but it does not thereby become a percentage of salary. The minimum wage follows yet another logic: there is no federal minimum wage, while some Cantons have their own. This parameter, too, cannot be confused with social-security contribution rates.
The formula attributed to Pamini therefore acquires a precise meaning only if it is clarified which base one wishes to modify. The source provides a general reference to contributions, but does not indicate whether the reference is social-security-related, insurance-related or linked to the labor market. Separating the three levels makes it possible to read the proposal without turning a headline into an already-defined fiscal measure. ## Cross-border commuters, cantons and documented limits
The word cross-border commuter is not enough to determine how each item is treated. Within the framework indicated by SEM, foreign permits are distinguished by function: permit L concerns short-term stays of up to one year, B is a renewable residence permit, C is a settlement permit normally linked to 10 years of residence or to 5 years for EU/EFTA citizens, while G identifies the cross-border commuter. These categories describe administrative status. The material does not say that the G permit alone automatically changes the AVS/AI/IPG, AD/AC, LAINF/LAA or LPP rates. Establishing an automatic link would be an undocumented step.
The rule provided on LAMal should be read with the same precision: it concerns residents, provides for the insurance obligation within three months of arrival and describes per-capita premiums, deductibles and cantonal reductions. It cannot be extended without further elements to those referred to in the title as cross-border commuters. The available text does not present specific rules for this category and does not indicate a different rate or a new healthcare tax.
### The work framework
Salaries and contributions also fall within the general rules governing the employment relationship. There is no federal minimum wage, although some cantons have their own. The maximum working time is 45 hours per week in industry, offices and retail, or 50 hours in other sectors. The minimum vacation entitlement is four weeks, five for those under 20. Maternity leave lasts 14 weeks at 80% through IPG; paternity leave lasts two weeks. The stated notice periods are one, two or three months, respectively, during the first year, from the second to the ninth year and from the tenth year.
These rules define the employment relationship, but do not demonstrate what intervention concerning contributions was proposed. Cantonal benefits and services also follow different rules: social assistance is generally administered by the cantons and municipalities based on need, while motor vehicle taxes, energy incentives, building permits and contributions to continuing education depend on the competent cantonal offices. Requirements, deadlines and amounts are not uniform throughout the country.
Amounts relating to the 3a third-pillar maximum, the threshold and the LPP coordination deduction, the AD/AC maximum, average LAMal premiums and the median salary must always be tied to the correct year, since they are subject to annual indexation.
Moving from percentages to the individual case therefore requires distinguishing salary, pension provision, insurance and taxes. salary/tax calculator is available for an operational comparison of deductions.

item.description: According to the national survey conducted by gfs.bern on behalf of economiesuisse and published today, 67% of the 1’527 companies surveyed consider
item.content:encoded:
## TL;DR - 67% consider the administrative burden high - 64% report an increase over five years - Three in ten companies postpone, reduce or cancel investments - More than 36’000 federal obligations burden companies
## Key facts - Research → gfs.bern on behalf of economiesuisse - Sample → 1’527 companies surveyed - Administrative burden → 67% consider it high - Increase → 64% over the last five years - Federal obligations → over 36’000
According to the national survey conducted by gfs.bern on behalf of economiesuisse and published today, 67% of the 1’527 companies surveyed consider the administrative burden high, as reported by Keystone-ATS.
In the same sample, 64% report an increase in bureaucracy over the last five years. Businesses complain about complex procedures and duplicate requests from the authorities. The research thus places side by side an assessment of the current burden and an assessment of the increase perceived over time.
The difference between 67% and 64% is three percentage points, but the two values are not interchangeable. The first indicates how many companies consider the burden high; the second indicates how many have observed growth over the five-year period specified by the source. Reading them separately makes it possible to avoid turning the comparison into a single measure of bureaucracy.
### The pressure measured on activities
The effects indicated include investment decisions: three out of ten Swiss companies have to postpone, scale back or cancel investments as a result of administrative constraints. The same constraints weigh particularly on the development of new products and services and on the training of apprentices. The source therefore establishes a link between administrative burdens, investment and internal training pathways, but does not offer any further breakdown of the sample. The issue thus affects both development and training activities and the management of procedures.
During a joint press conference, Silvan Wildhaber, president of economiesuisse, described the growing burden as “a problem made at home” that must be corrected to preserve jobs and prosperity, according to the written version of his speech. The news report presents this position together with the research findings: the survey describes the companies’ assessments, while the president identifies correcting the burden as an objective for the economy. ## Comparison between perception and impact
### Three measures that should not be conflated
In the available text, the three results are not interchangeable. The sample is the same, consisting of 1’527 companies, but each figure answers a different question: the level of the burden, the trend in bureaucracy, and investment decisions. The correct comparison starts from this distinction.
| Indicator | What it measures | Figure | |---|---|---| | Administrative burden | Level considered high | 67% | | Bureaucracy | Increase over the last five years | 64% | | Investments | Postponement, reduction or cancellation | Three in ten companies |
The gap between 67% and 64% is therefore three percentage points. It does not, however, justify adding the percentages together or treating them as a single measure. The 67% describes the share that considers the burden high; the 64% the share that reports an increase over the last five years. The first figure concerns the level, the second the perceived change.
The figure of three in ten companies concerns a third dimension: it does not measure a perception, but a decision that companies say they are forced to make because of administrative constraints. The source does not indicate how many of these companies are also part of the 67% or 64%. It is therefore not possible to infer an overlap between the groups from the numbers alone.
The survey is national, but the available text does not break down the results by economic sector or geographic area. The figure should therefore be read as the result for the sample as a whole, not as a ranking among sectors or areas.
The link between problems and requests, by contrast, is explicit. Complex procedures and duplicate requests are associated with the complete digitization of administrative processes, standardized forms and one-stop shops at all levels of government. The principle of submitting data only once is also linked to the problem of duplication. This comparison describes a correspondence between the issues identified and the solutions requested by the business community; it does not yet document an outcome that has already been achieved. ## Requests from the associations
### Voices from the various economic sectors
Concerns affect several sectors. Annette Luther, president of scienceindustries, emphasized the need to accelerate approval procedures for chemical and pharmaceutical innovation. In the technology sector, Martin Hirzel, president of Swissmem, pointed to narrower margins and rising regulatory costs. Stefan Mäder, president of the Swiss Insurance Association, believes that the competitiveness of the economic hub should be an explicit objective of regulations.
The three statements point to distinct pressure points. In the chemical and pharmaceutical sector, the focus is on the speed of approvals; in the technology sector, the issue is associated with margins and regulatory costs; for insurance, the topic concerns the objective assigned to regulation. The source does not present these positions as separate survey data, but as concerns expressed by the leaders of different economic sectors.
### From managing forms to rules
The business community proposes fully digitizing administrative procedures, supplemented by standardized forms and a single point of access for each level of public administration. The measures would thus affect both the management of procedures and relations with the authorities. The associations are also calling for a reduction in regulation—the federal obligations imposed on companies exceed 36’000—and for the single-submission principle for data to be applied.
The broader economic framework also forms part of the requests: there are calls to eliminate technical barriers to trade, support agreements such as Bilateral III, and adopt a risk-oriented regulatory approach rather than one based on detailed prescription. The text thus places measures concerning administrative processes alongside proposals relating to regulation, trade and international relations.
The source documents requests from the associations and statements by their representatives, not the adoption of a measure already in force. It does not provide a timetable for digitizing, standardizing the forms, or reducing the obligations. The verifiable fact is therefore the importance attributed by companies to bureaucracy and the package of measures that the business community proposes to reduce it.
*Source: [swissinfo.ch](https://www.swissinfo.ch/ita/cresce-il-peso-della-burocrazia-sulle-imprese-in-svizzera/92349489)*

item.title: 5% substitute tax on Swiss pensions
item.description: In response No. 125/2024, the Italian Revenue Agency examined the tax treatment of benefits paid by the Swiss pension schemes of the first pillar AVS
item.content:encoded:
## TL;DR - Response no. 125/2024 concerns Swiss pensions - AVS as a monthly annuity, LPP as a one-off lump-sum redemption - The substitute tax provided for is 5%
## Key facts - Regulation → Article 76 of Law no. 413 of 30 December 1991 - Institutions Revenue → Agency, AVS and LPP - AVS → first pillar and monthly income - LPP → second pillar and one-time redemption - Rate → 5%
In response no. 125/2024, the Revenue Agency examined the tax treatment of benefits paid by the Swiss social security schemes of the first AVS pillar and the second LPP pillar. The clarification concerns those who receive pension income from the Swiss Confederation and intend to transfer their tax residence to Italy.
### The case examined
After carrying out an employment activity in Switzerland and paying the related contributions, the taxpayer had decided to move to Italy, changing his residence. He had also requested the advance payment of the AVS, which was expected to be paid in the form of a monthly annuity.
The method envisaged for the sums of the LPP management was different. The second pillar would be liquidated in the form of a one-time ransom. The difference between income and capital led the taxpayer to ask the Revenue Agency how to apply Article 76 of Law no. 413 of 30 December 1991, as subsequently amended.
The question concerned in particular the entire amount of the sums relating to the second Swiss pillar. The applicant asked if the substitute taxation of 5% could include both the mandatory and the over-compulsory part, according to the terminology of Swiss legislation.
In the proposed interpretative solution, the taxpayer believed that the same rate should be applied to the two benefits: to the annuity paid by the AVS insurance and to the entire capital paid by the LPP management. The administration's response therefore addresses both forms of disbursement and their connection with Italian tax discipline. ## The framework between the Convention and Italian law
Articles 18 and 21 of the Convention between Italy and Switzerland constitute, according to the tax administration, the first point of reference for determining where pension income is to be taxed. The international treaty was ratified by Law no. 943/1978. The provisions referred to establish that pensions are taxed exclusively in the recipient's State of residence, excluding double taxation on the sums received.
### Two levels to distinguish
The Convention identifies the State of residence entitled to levy the tax. Italian domestic legislation, on the other hand, defines the substitute tax treatment applicable to pension benefits. In the case described, the person had transferred their residence to Italy, while the benefits derived from Swiss social security schemes.
| Scheme | Pillar | Form described | Treatment indicated | |---|---|---|---| | AVS | First | Monthly annuity | 5% substitute tax | | LPP | Second | One-off lump-sum redemption | 5% substitute tax, including the mandatory and over-mandatory portions |
Paragraph 1-ter of Article 76 of Law 413/91, referred to by the administration, extends substitute taxation at a rate of 5% to sums paid anywhere by insurance for disability, old age and survivors, identified by the acronym AVS. The same provision also covers the occupational pension scheme for old age, survivors and disability, identified by the acronym LPP.
The text also includes benefits paid by Swiss early-retirement bodies or institutions, when accrued also on the basis of social security contributions taxed at source in the Confederation. For the question submitted to the Italian Revenue Agency, this passage means that the distinction between the mandatory and over-mandatory component of the second pillar does not exclude the latter from the scope of the indicated rate.
The comparison between AVS and LPP therefore does not describe two different rates. Instead, it highlights two payment methods, a monthly annuity and a one-off capital payment, which the response brings under the same substitute regime provided for Swiss pensions. ## Declaration, payment and limits of the clarification
The Revenue Agency's response also addresses the methods for fulfilling tax and declaration obligations. The taxpayer can self-assess the tax due in the declaration, indicate the sums collected in the reference year and pay the amount using Form F24, with tax code 1242.
### The operational data indicated by the source
The procedure described links the calculation to the amount of sums actually collected in the year considered. The form of payment remains distinct: the AVS in the examined case would have been received as a monthly income, while the LPP would have been paid on a one-off basis. However, the answer deals with both services within the scope of the 5% substitute tax.
The text does not report a concrete pension amount or a numerical simulation. Instead, the regulatory basis, the two Swiss social security management systems, the tax residence taken into consideration and the tax code to be used for the payment are indicated. This delimits what the reconstruction allows to affirm without further calculations on the individual perceiver.
A further distinction concerns the 25% that appear in the list of source-related content. That percentage refers to a different measure: the cross-border commuter flat tax indicated as applicable from 2027, equal to 25% of taxes paid in Switzerland. It is not the rate presented in answer no. 125/2024 for AVS and LPP pensions, for which the text examines 5%.
For the official documentation on the AVS, the [AVS Synoptic Table 2026] is available (https://www.ahv-iv.ch/p/2.01.i). To find your way between AVS, LPP and annuity, AVS and LPP is available.

item.title: People vote on VAT increase to cover AVS 13th-pension costs
item.description: On November 29, the people will be called upon to vote on the VAT increase chosen by the Federal Parliament to help cover the costs of the 13th AHV
item.content:encoded:
## TL;DR
- The people approved the 13th AVS pension - On November 29, there will be a vote on the VAT increase - The Federal Parliament chose VAT to cover the costs - The reduced rate for essential goods remains unchanged
## Key facts
- Signatory → Sara Demir, cantonal parliamentarian for il Centro - Benefit → thirteenth AVS pension - Date → November 29 - Parliamentary decision → increase in VAT - Coming years → further decisions and AVS 2030 reform
On November 29, voters will be called upon to vote on the increase in VAT chosen by the Federal Parliament to help cover the costs of the thirteenth AVS pension. Sara Demir, cantonal parliamentarian for il Centro, considers this step a difficult but necessary choice following approval of the new benefit.
### The decision to be funded
The sequence outlined in her remarks is clear: first, voters approved the thirteenth AVS pension; then the issue of funding arose. Old-age provision is described as one of the foundations of Swiss solidarity; the next question concerns how to sustain the benefits introduced over time.
Demir does not present the increase in VAT as an ideal solution. Her reasoning is based on the lack of cost-free solutions and the need to distribute the burden without further penalizing those who work and produce.
> “There are no shortcuts: we need to decide how to distribute the costs without further penalizing those who work and produce.”
The first alternative she rejects is a further increase in payroll contributions. According to the cantonal parliamentarian, this path would further reduce people’s net wages and increase companies’ costs. She also points to the Canton of Ticino, where many companies operate in a challenging competitive environment.
The second caveat concerns the retirement age. Demir acknowledges that those who wish and are able to continue working should be supported, but she does not consider it right to base the sustainability of the AVS on the idea that everyone should extend their working lives. As she points out, working conditions are not the same: for those who perform physically demanding tasks, reaching the end of their working lives in good condition can be more difficult.
The November vote is therefore presented as a decision on funding a benefit that has already been approved, not as the definitive solution for the AVS. ## Comparing the alternatives
Demir's statement builds the comparison around the stated effects and limitations, not around a numerical calculation. The verifiable connection therefore concerns the basis on which the burden would fall and the limitation that the Grand Council member associates with each option.
### What the source compares
| Option | Stated base | Reported effect or limitation | |---|---|---| | Payroll contributions | Workers and companies | Lower net pay and higher burdens for companies | | Increase in the retirement age | Length of working life | Working conditions are not the same | | VAT | Consumption, individuals and families | The cost also falls on consumption; the reduced rate remains unchanged | | Tobacco and alcohol | Specific consumption | It cannot be assumed that revenues alone will be sufficient |
In the case of VAT, the statement simultaneously asserts that the increase would entail a cost for individuals and families and that the burden would also be spread beyond labour and wages. This is the concrete connection supporting the stated preference: not a promise of zero cost, but the choice to avoid concentrating all funding on labour and companies. The fact that the reduced rate for essential goods and services remains unchanged also limits the effect described, without eliminating it.
The comparison with the retirement age follows an explicit criterion. The statement does not dispute that some people may continue working for a long time; it disputes the idea that this possibility could become an automatic response for everyone. The distinction concerns working conditions: those who perform physically demanding tasks may face greater difficulty reaching the end of their careers in good condition. Hence the preference for measures that support those who want to and are able to work longer, without turning this choice into a general obligation.
The proposal concerning tobacco and alcohol plays a different role. It is not presented as an already sufficient alternative, but as a possibility that the Federal Council should seriously assess through a review of taxation. The reference to the 13th pension's multibillion costs sets the limit of the proposal: according to Demir, those revenues cannot be considered sufficient on their own to cover them.
The phrase 'the lesser evil' therefore has a precise meaning in the statement: it does not mean that VAT is harmless, but that, among the alternatives considered, Demir prefers neither to place a further burden on labour nor to use the extension of working life as an automatic response. ## The AVS dossier remains open
The passage of November 29th does not close the discussion. In Demir's argument, the possible increase in VAT would help finance the new benefit, but would not by itself solve all the financial challenges of the AVS. Further decisions would be needed in the coming years and the 2030 AVS reform should be approached seriously.
### The limit of the proposed solution
The limit is not presented as a technical detail, but as a political condition. An important performance must be able to be sustained over time. For this reason, the responsibility of politics is measured on several fronts: the security of retired people, the possibility for those who work to contribute without being continually burdened by new costs and the confidence of younger generations in the future.
The intervention does not provide a VAT rate, a figure per household or a breakdown of costs between individuals, families, workers and companies. It therefore does not allow us to transform the preference for VAT into an individual calculation, nor to say what the concrete effect would be on the consumption of a single family. The documented data is more limited: the increase would have a cost for individuals and families, while the reduced rate for basic necessities and services would remain unchanged.
The same limit applies to income from tobacco and alcohol. Demir asks the Federal Council to seriously address the possibility of a revision of the taxation on these products, but does not present an estimate of the revenue. The text only allows us to report two points: the road deserves attention and, given the billion-dollar cost of the thirteenth income, it cannot be assumed that it is enough on its own.
The distinction between contribution and complete solution avoids attributing to the vote a result that the intervention does not promise. The federal parliament chose VAT to help cover the costs of the new service; the sustainability of the entire system remains linked to subsequent decisions. Even the invitation to discuss the AVS 2030 indicates that the financing of the thirteenth annuity is still an open chapter.
For the official reference indicated on the AVS, the [SYnoptic table AVS 2026] is available (https://www.ahv-iv.ch/p/2.01.i). To learn more about income, consult AVS and pension.
*Source: [tio.ch](https://www.tio.ch/rubriche/ospite/1961525/avs-iva-costo-demir-sara)*

item.description: According to data released on Thursday by the State Secretariat for Economic Affairs (SECO), the number of people registered with the Regional
item.content:encoded:
## TL;DR - URC registrations at 141’015: up 0,4% in October - Unemployment rate steady at 3% - Young people: 679 fewer unemployed people, rate at 3,2% - Vacancies at 40’462, down 8,5%
## Key facts | Term | Value | | --- | --- | | Period | October | | Registered with the RCOs | 141’015; +0,4%, equal to 535 people | | Unemployment rate | 3% | | Seasonally adjusted rate | 3,1% | | Unemployed young people | -679; -4,7%; rate at 3,2% | | People seeking work | 230’001; rate at 4,9% | | Vacancies | 40’462; -8,5% | | Short-time work | 7’068 people in July |
### The October figure According to data released on Thursday by the State Secretariat for Economic Affairs (SECO), in October the number of people registered with the Regional Employment Centres (RCOs) increased by 535 compared with September. The increase is 0,4%, bringing the total to 141’015. The month-on-month comparison therefore shows a limited change, not a jump in the number of people reported as unemployed.
The unemployment rate remained at 3% compared with September. Alongside the ordinary rate, the statement also gives the percentage calculated excluding seasonal effects: in October, both remained unchanged from September, but the second figure was 3,1%.
The breakdown by age, however, shows a different movement. The number of unemployed young people fell by 679, or 4,7%, and their rate declined by 0,1 percentage points, to 3,2%. Among older people, by contrast, the number registered with the RCOs increased by 239, or 0,6%, to 38’721. The corresponding rate rose from 2,6% in September to 2,7%.
The overall figure therefore does not represent a uniform movement among the groups observed: the younger component declined, the older component increased, while the general rate remained unchanged. SECO’s communication describes these changes but does not attribute a cause to them. The comparison with September should therefore be read separately for the total, the seasonally adjusted figure and the age groups. ## Three indicators, three readings The number of people registered with the URC does not automatically coincide with the number of people looking for work or with the number of vacancies: the release presents them as distinct measures. This separation is useful for interpreting October without attributing the entire trend in the labor market to the 3% rate alone.
### The figures are not interchangeable | Indicator | October | Comparison with the previous month | | --- | --- | --- | | People registered with the URC | 141’015 | +535 people; +0,4% compared with September | | People looking for work | 230’001 | increase of 1,1%; rate at 4,9%, up from 4,8% | | Vacancies | 40’462 | decrease of 8,5% |
The picture that emerges from the table is misaligned: URC registrations increase slightly, the number of people looking for work rises by 1,1%, while vacancies decrease by 8,5%. The rate associated with people looking for work rises from 4,8% to 4,9%, so it does not follow the stability of the unemployment rate. The source does not present these changes as causing one another and does not make it possible to infer an automatic effect on the number of hires.
A purely arithmetic comparison helps measure the distance between the figures: for October, 230’001 ÷ 40’462 is approximately 5,7. It is only a descriptive ratio, not a placement rate. The text does not state that every person looking for work is a candidate for every position, nor that the two series have the same composition.
Of the 40’462 vacancies, 25’803 fall under the reporting requirement, introduced in 2018 for sectors with high unemployment. The figure adds detail about the composition of job openings, but does not indicate which occupations or which geographic areas are involved. ## Other signals, but for different periods The data on short-time work and the exhaustion of entitlement to unemployment benefits supplement the release, but do not pertain to the same month as the main figure. Short-time work refers to July, while the exhaustion of entitlement refers to August; the unemployment rate and those registered with the URCs, on the other hand, concern October.
### July and August In July, short-time work affected 7’068 people: 1’295 fewer than in the previous month. The number of sectors affected by reduced working hours fell by more than a quarter, to 473. These are two different measures: one counts the people involved, while the other counts the sectors in which the reduction was recorded.
In August, 2’718 people exhausted their entitlement to unemployment benefits, 9,5% fewer than in July. The comparison is therefore between August and July, while the comparison of those registered with the URCs is between October and September. Mixing these time bases would produce a single reading that the source does not present.
The reported content does not indicate the causes of the changes, does not make forecasts for the following months, and does not offer a breakdown by regions, professions, or individual sectors. It therefore does not document a causal link between the reduction in working hours in July, the exhaustion of benefits in August, and the unemployment rate in October. SECO provides a series of indicators to be read separately, with their respective reference period.

item.title: Teleworking and cross-border workers: Swiss rules
item.description: Switzerland levies taxes at three levels: direct federal tax, cantonal tax and municipal tax.
item.content:encoded:
## TL;DR - The Swiss tax system has three levels - AVS/AI/IPG: 5,3% borne by the employee - LAMal is mandatory for anyone residing in Switzerland - Many services depend on cantons and municipalities
## Key facts - Federal, cantonal and municipal → IFD tax - AVS/AI/IPG → 5.3% employee; 10.6% total - AD/AC → 1.1% up to the annual ceiling - Permit G → category for frontier workers - Rental deposit → maximum three months
### The Swiss system separates tax and social security
Switzerland organises the tax levy on three levels: direct federal tax, cantonal tax and municipal tax. Each Canton applies its own law and its own multiplier; the municipality uses a multiplier on the cantonal tax. For cross-border teleworking, this architecture is the starting point so as not to confuse the responsibilities of the offices with the job position.
The AFC/ESTV deals with direct federal tax and VAT. Cantonal administrations, on the other hand, manage cantonal and municipal taxation. The UFAS/BSV covers social security, including AVS/AI and LPP/BVG, but does not set taxes. The UST/BFS produces statistics and does not establish rates. The distinction is also useful when a worker reads a contract or a paycheck: a social contribution and a tax are not the same item nor are they at the same institutional level.
On salary, AVS/AI/IPG provide for 5.3% to be borne by the employee and 10.6% overall with the employer. The AD/AC is equal to 1.1% up to the annual ceiling. LAINF/LAA ranges from 0.7% to 1.5% depending on the sector. For the LPP/BVG, applied to the coordinated salary, the indicated rates are 7% between 25 and 34 years, 10% between 35 and 44, 15% between 45 and 54 and 18% from 55 years up to the reference age. These parameters are distinct from the municipal tax and the sick pay premium.
### Residence, health and permits
LAMal/KVG is the mandatory health insurance for residents. It must be stipulated within three months of arrival; the premium is per capita, not a tax and not a salary contribution. Premiums vary by Canton and region, while premium reduction is a cantonal subsidy. For adults, the deductibles are CHF 300, 500, 1000, 1500, 2000 or 2500.
According to the SEM, the L title covers short-term stays, up to one year, while the B permit concerns the residence and is renewable. Permit C certifies domicile and permit G is intended for frontier workers. In general, the C permit is obtained after ten years of residence; for EU/EFTA citizens the ordinary period is five years. Permits define residence status, without determining tax and social security obligations on their own. ## Comparing a deduction with a premium The most useful difference for those working across the border and teleworking concerns the basis on which the burden arises. AVS/AI/IPG, AD/AC, LAINF/LAA contributions and LPP/BVG are expressed as percentages of the salary or coordinated salary. LAMal/KVG, however, follows per capita premiums, differentiated by canton and region. Putting everything under the generic heading 'taxes' can alter the reading of remuneration and cost of living because the system uses different bases and authorities.
### A skills map
| Area | Verified rule | Competent level | |---|---|---| | IFD and VAT | Federal levies | AFC/ESTV | | Cantonal and municipal tax | Each canton has its own law and multiplier; the municipality applies a multiplier on the cantonal one | Cantonal administrations | | Social security | AVS/AI/LPP and social security | UFAS/BSV | | LAMal/KVG | Mandatory for residents; per capita premiums per canton and region; cantonal premium reduction | Canton for the subsidy | | Permits | L, B, C, and G with different characteristics | SEM | | Statistics | Statistical data, not rates | UST/BFS |
The map helps understand which question can be answered by which level. A query on VAT or direct federal tax does not have the same reference authority as a question on the municipal multiplier. Similarly, UFAS/BSV concerns social security and does not decide tax rates. For the social security part and references on teleworking, the official reference provided is the [UFAS](https://www.bsv.admin.ch/it/telelavoro) page.
The G permit identifies the category of cross-border workers, but the provided framework does not associate a specific teleworking percentage with this designation. Therefore, the mere residence permit does not allow deriving a tax or social security amount other than what is indicated in the available data. The distinction between residence, work, and social security must be kept separate even when the activity is distributed across multiple locations.
### The house follows a different logic
Tenancy is regulated by federal law, uniform in every canton, through CO art. 253 et seq. The security deposit cannot exceed three months' rent and must be paid into a blocked account in the tenant's name. The landlord's notice of termination is valid only if it uses the official cantonal form. The tenant can contest it within 30 days before the conciliation authority.
This comparison shows a recurring combination in the Swiss system: the basic rule may be federal, while the form, subsidy, multiplier, or competent office may depend on the canton or municipality. For cross-border teleworking, reading these areas separately avoids turning a payslip data point into an automatic conclusion about housing, health, or taxes. ## The employment relationship has a common basis, but no federal minimum wage
In Switzerland there is no federal minimum wage; some cantons have their own. The maximum working week is 45 hours in industry, offices and retail, or 50 hours in other sectors. The minimum vacation entitlement is four weeks, rising to five for those under 20.
The national rules indicated also include 14 weeks of maternity leave at 80% through IPG and two weeks of paternity leave. For termination, the reported notice periods are one month in the first year, two months from the second through the ninth, and three months from the tenth. These parameters describe the employment relationship and are not a measure of the share of work carried out remotely.
### Services that vary from one canton to another
As a rule, social assistance is administered by cantons and municipalities according to need. Motor vehicle tax, energy incentives, building permits and contributions to continuing education are likewise governed by cantonal rules and offices. Requirements, deadlines and amounts must therefore be checked with the relevant official source, rather than inferred from a single national rule.
Several services are regulated at the territorial level. Building insurance may be mandatory or organized differently depending on the canton. Civil protection, although it falls within the framework of federal law, is coordinated at cantonal level: call-ups and allowances must be checked with the competent authority.
### Indexed figures should not be set without a year
Some values change every year: the maximum for the 3a third pillar, the LPP coordination threshold or deduction, the AD/AC maximum, average LAMal premiums and the median salary. The verified framework does not provide precise amounts that can be applied without specifying the year, so it is not correct to turn these quantities into permanent figures.
The same limitation applies to cross-border telework. The available data do not include a single percentage threshold, nor a general amount or deadline that would make it possible to automatically calculate the tax and social-security impact of the portion performed remotely. The responsibilities, contribution bases, the LAMal rule for residents, permit categories and cantonal differences are defined instead. For an indicative calculation of the ratio between remuneration and charges, the salary and tax calculator is available.

item.title: VAT increase: UBS study highlights greater impact on low-income households
item.description: In Zurich, on November 6, 2026, a UBS analysis examined the proposed increase in value-added tax, VAT, to partially finance the 13th AVS/AHV pension
item.content:encoded:
## TL;DR - UBS: VAT weighs more heavily on low-income households - From January 1, 2028: 8,1% would rise to 8,5% - The popular vote is scheduled for November 29 - Second quintile: 3,4% of saving capacity
## Key facts - Who → UBS - Measure → VAT increase for the 13th AVS pension - Vote → November 29 - First payment → December 2026 - Proposed effective date → January 1, 2028 - Standard rate → from 8,1% to 8,5% - Special rate → from 3,8% to 4% - Reduced rate → 2,6% unchanged
## The proposal put to the vote
In Zurich, on November 6, 2026, a UBS analysis examined the proposed increase in value added tax (VAT) to partially fund the 13th AVS/AHV pension. The measure will be put to a popular vote on November 29. According to the study, the increase would affect all Swiss households, but lower-income families would be more severely affected.
The most exposed aspect identified by the analysis is the ability of the most economically vulnerable households to save. The study is based on data from the Federal Statistical Office (UST/BFS) and links VAT to available resources and the ability to set money aside.
### The proposal timeline
The introduction of the 13th AVS pension was approved by Swiss voters in March 2024. The benefit will be paid for the first time in December 2026. To cover part of its costs, the Confederation proposes increasing VAT.
If the federal decree were to receive the double majority of the people and the cantons, from January 1, 2028, the standard rate would increase from 8,1% to 8,5%. The special rate would rise from 3,8% to 4%, while the reduced rate would remain unchanged at 2,6%.
The timeline distinguishes three stages: the approval of the 13th pension, which has already taken place; the first payment in December 2026; and the possible change to the rates from January 1, 2028. The source explicitly refers to partial funding of the pension.
### The subject of the analysis
The report considers not only the additional expenditure, but also its impact on households' economic situation. For the most vulnerable households, the effect could manifest itself primarily in a reduction in the margin available for saving. Households with greater financial resources, on the other hand, might continue to set money aside, albeit potentially to a lesser extent.
This is the main link between the increase in VAT and households' financial lives: the proposal is assessed not only by the amount of the tax, but also by the share of resources that would remain available after expenses and by the ability to set money aside. ## The comparison between income and savings
The analysis presents two distinct comparisons. The first uses the current rates and measures the VAT paid over a year relative to disposable income. The second considers the additional expenditure associated with the proposed increase and expresses it as a share of saving capacity. The two measures therefore refer to explicitly different bases in the source: on the one hand, disposable income; on the other, the amount a household is able to set aside.
For a single person under 65 with an annual gross income of 50'000 francs, the VAT paid at the current rates amounts to approximately 1'404 francs per year. The expenditure is equivalent to 3,9% of disposable income. For a person with an annual gross income of 150'000 francs, VAT rises to 2'746 francs, but its share falls to 2,8%.
| Person | Annual gross income | Annual VAT | Share of disposable income | |---|---:|---:|---:| | Single person, under 65 | 50'000 francs | approximately 1'404 francs | 3,9% | | Single person, under 65 | 150'000 francs | approximately 2'746 francs | 2,8% |
The comparison shows the regressive nature of VAT described by UBS. In absolute terms, the person with the higher income pays more. Relative to available resources, however, the share is lower: the change from 3,9% to 2,8% is the figure used by the study to highlight the difference in proportional incidence.
### The burden on saving capacity
To measure the effect of the proposed increase, the source relates the additional expenditure to saving capacity. For a single person under 65 belonging to the second-lowest income quintile, the burden would account for approximately 3,4% of that capacity; for the same type of household in the highest income bracket, the share would be 0,4%.
The figure is particularly significant for lower-income households, which often already cannot save or face considerable difficulty doing so. The report warns that the increase could further squeeze their financial margins, leaving them to choose between lower saving capacity and reduced consumption.
According to the source, the average impact on household budgets would be comparable to a 1,7% increase in compulsory health insurance premiums, namely LAMal/KVG. The figure is merely a reference and does not announce an actual increase in premiums. As for the cost of living, the estimate therefore remains limited to the effects on household budgets, VAT, and saving capacity. ## The 13th AVS and the financing limits
A possible paradox emerges in the UBS report: the 13th pension will support some pensioners with limited resources, but they will have to face a higher VAT burden in relation to their financial situation. The new benefit is therefore not presented as a solution to all the economic problems of pensioners; the title of the section dedicated to the measure makes it clear that the 13th AVS will not solve every difficulty.
The tension arises from the fact that the proposed financing would be distributed through VAT, a tax which according to the analysis weighs proportionately more on low incomes. The same group of people could therefore receive support from the annuity and face, in the same financial framework, a higher VAT burden compared to their resources.
### The alternative of wage contributions
Among the options evaluated in Parliament also includes the increase in wage contributions. According to BAK Economics estimates, increasing the standard VAT rate by one percentage point, while also proportionally adjusting the other rates, would generate resources equal to those of an increase of approximately 0.75 points in salary contributions.
The reference to BAK Economics serves to compare two financing methods: the increase in VAT and the increase in wage contributions. The source presents this hypothesis as one of the alternatives discussed in Parliament and does not state that it has been chosen.
### A yes would not close the file
A favorable outcome of the vote may therefore not be enough: according to the study, to finance the 13th pension and guarantee the stability of the AVS, further measures will most likely be necessary. Insurance finances also remain under pressure due to demographic changes.
The outcome of the vote would therefore concern VAT rates, but the report places the decision within a broader financial question. To come into force, the proposal would have to obtain a double majority of the people and the cantons; only in that case, from 1 January 2028, would the steps indicated for the normal, special and reduced rates come into force.
The available figures allow the incidence of the tax to be compared, but not to attribute an identical additional amount to each household. The analysis reports annual VAT amounts at current rates for two income levels and, for the proposed increase, percentages referring to saving capacity and family budgets. For the institutional framework of social security, the [AVS 2026 synoptic table] is available (https://www.ahv-iv.ch/p/2.01.i).

item.title: Electricity reserve: CDF identifies savings of 220 million
item.description: The CDF puts the untapped savings potential in establishing the electricity reserve for the winter at 220 million francs.
item.content:encoded:
## TL;DR - The CDF sees 220 million francs in potential savings - The plan calls for four power plants starting in 2030 - Planned expenditure is 2,18 billion francs - The project is pending in Parliament
## Key facts - Potential identified by the CDF → 220 million francs - Funding planned by the Federal Council → 2,18 billion from 2030 - Planned power plants → four reserve power plants - Deviation from the recommended minimum → 83 megawatts - Project status → pending in Parliament
The CDF estimates that 220 million francs in savings potential remains untapped in establishing the winter electricity reserve. The report examines the composition and sizing of the reserve, not the procurement of capacity, which would instead have been carried out cost-effectively.
### What the report criticizes
The CDF points to two factors. Emergency generator sets, which the report considers potentially more economical, would not be treated as a type of reserve. In addition, excessive sizing of the reserve generates additional costs. In the audit body's view, less costly alternatives could help avert an electricity shortage and thus fulfill the reserve's main purpose.
At the same time, the Federal Council intends to allocate 2,18 billion francs from 2030 for four reserve power plants. The Government's stated objective is to prevent possible shortages. According to the Government, the costs would be neutral for the federal budget because they would be billed directly to end consumers.
The project remains pending in Parliament. The review by the competent committee of the National Council is contingent on the availability of a new assessment by the Federal Electricity Commission (ElCom) on the security of electricity supply, which the committee expects next spring. The source does not yet indicate a final decision on the type of reserve or its configuration. ## Comparison of expenditure and potential savings
The CDF's report compares planned expenditure, a potential savings margin and a difference in capacity. These are different quantities: putting them side by side does not mean that the 220 million have already been recovered or that they represent a reduction that has already been decided on.
| Item | Value | Reference in the source | |---|---:|---| | Potential savings | 220 million francs | CDF | | Planned expenditure | 2,18 billion francs from 2030 | four reserve power plants | | Excess over the minimum | 83 megawatts | reserve recommended for 2030 |
Purely arithmetically, 220 million francs amount to approximately 10,1% of the planned 2,18 billion francs. The calculation helps show the proportion between the two amounts, but does not describe savings already realized or change the fact that the project is still pending in Parliament.
For end consumers, the connection documented in the text is direct but limited: the Government expects the costs of the four power plants to be billed directly to them. The source does not specify the allocation method, the share attributable to a single household or company, or the billing date. It is therefore not possible to turn the potential indicated by the CDF into a specific increase in francs for each consumer.
### The issue of alternatives
The economic comparison mainly concerns the role of emergency generator sets. In the CDF's view, these are potentially cheaper resources that could help avert a shortage and thus fulfill the reserve's main purpose. According to the UFE, however, the limited possibilities for using the generator sets would prevent that savings potential from being realized.
According to the UFE, these facilities could only supplement the reserve power plants, not replace them. The disagreement therefore concerns the role these generator sets could play in the reserve's overall structure and the resulting sizing of the planned power plants. ## The safety margin and the parliamentary process
The discussion concerns more than just the cost of the various options. The SFAO also notes that the four reserve power plants envisaged in the Federal Council's proposal exceed the minimum level recommended for 2030 by 83 megawatts. To limit expenditure, the audit body adds, available reserves should be sized to the absolute minimum necessary.
However, the Federal Electricity Commission draws attention to risk prevention and to the possibility that the reserve requirement may prove greater at a later stage. The dossier therefore contains two different indications: on the one hand, the request to keep the reserve within the recommended minimum level; on the other, caution linked to a possible greater need.
### Renewables and expected assessment
The SFAO also reiterates that growth in renewable energy in line with the targets set could considerably reduce the need for reserves in late winter, to the point of making recourse to reserves unnecessary. The wording is conditional: the source does not claim that this reduction has already occurred, nor does it quantify the possible savings associated with this development.
Politically, the proposal to make the four power plants available is currently pending in Parliament. Before examining the proposal, the competent committee of the National Council wants a new assessment from ElCom on the security of electricity supply. According to the committee, the document is expected next spring.
Several elements therefore remain open: the final choice of reserve types, the final sizing of the power plants, the possible role of emergency generator sets and the outcome of the new ElCom assessment. The text indicates neither a final parliamentary decision nor the amount that would be charged to each end consumer.

item.title: LPP pension provision: interest rate of 2% from Jan. 1, 2027
item.description: From January 2027, the minimum interest rate for the second pillar will rise from 1,25% to 2%, according to the decision of the Federal Council.
item.content:encoded:
## TL;DR - From January 2027, the minimum rate will rise to 2% - The current rate is 1,25% - Institution returns: 6,1% in 2025 and 5,4% in 2026 - Average coverage: 122,5% at the end of August 2026
## Key facts Decision → Federal Council Scope → second pillar, BVG Effective → January 2027 New minimum rate → 2% BVG fee recommendation → 1.75% Social partners' proposals → between 1.25% and 3% Average return of institutions → 6.1% in 2025; 5.4% in 2026, until the end of August Average reach → 122.5% at the end of August 2026
From January 2027, the minimum interest rate for the second pillar will rise from 1.25% to 2%, as decided by the Federal Council. The measure is part of the occupational pension system regulated by the BVG, the federal law dedicated to retirement, survivors' and disability pensions.
Prior to the decision, the BVG committee had recommended a rate of 1.75%, while the social partners had proposed values of between 1.25% and 3%. The 2% approved by the Federal Council thus exceeds the committee's indication, but remains within the range supported by the social partners.
### The criterion used to set the minimum
To determine the minimum rate, the yields on federal bonds, equities and real estate are assessed. The government reported in a statement on Wednesday that the overall development of these three components was positive in both 2025 and 2026.
The Federal Social Insurance Office (FSIO) estimates that the average return on pension funds in 2025 is 6.1% and that of 2026 at 5.4% until the end of August. According to the government, this allows for a significant increase in the minimum interest rate and compensates for the relatively high inflation observed since 2022. The source therefore reports both the overall yield figure and the average of the institutions as elements of the picture. ## The comparison between the rate and returns
Arithmetically, the change from 1,25% to 2% amounts to 0,75 percentage points. Compared with the 1,75% recommended by the commission, the difference is 0,25 percentage points. The 2% also lies within the range between 1,25% and 3% indicated by the social partners. These are comparisons calculated from the source values, not additional rates decided by the Federal Council.
### The indicators in the two periods
The minimum-rate criterion can be understood by comparing the results given for institutions and markets. The table retains the units and time windows present in the source.
| Indicator | 2025 | 2026 | |---|---:|---:| | Average return of pension institutions | 6,1% | 5,4%, through the end of August | | Swiss Performance Index | increase of 17,8% | increase of 7,6%, through the end of September | | Swiss Bond Domestic AAA - BBB | lost 0,2% | lost 1,1%, through the end of September |
The comparison does not have a single closing date for 2026: the estimate for the institutions runs through the end of August, while the two market indicators run through the end of September. This time limitation must be retained when comparing 2025 and 2026. The Swiss Performance Index increased in both periods considered, while the Swiss Bond Domestic AAA - BBB recorded a loss in both; real estate, on the other hand, showed a consistently positive trend. The source therefore describes an overall positive picture, but with different results among equities, bonds and real estate.
The figure for Confederation bonds also provides a separate comparison. The interest rate paid on ten-year bonds was 0,33% at the end of 2025 and 0,59% at the end of September 2026. These are two values referring to the same type of maturity, but at two different points in time. Comparing them with equity and real estate returns clarifies which indicators are cited to set the minimum rate, without turning the partial data for 2026 into a forecast. ## The coverage of institutions and the limits of the framework
UFAS estimates indicated, at the end of August 2026, an average coverage ratio of 122.5% for pension institutions without state guarantee. The data indicates that, on average, these institutions had value fluctuation reserves and means greater than those necessary to fulfill their obligations.
### An average data, with partial periods
The wording refers to the average and institutions without state guarantee. The 122.5% is not presented as the coverage ratio of each individual institution. The text also does not provide individual results, amounts per person or an estimate of the effect of the new rate on specific annuities. These elements remain outside the information reported.
The same scope applies to yield data. For 2026, the average performance of the institutions is calculated until the end of August, while the progression of the Swiss Performance Index and the result of the Swiss Bond Domestic AAA - BBB arrive until the end of September. The source therefore speaks of estimates and periods not yet closed in the same way; does not indicate a definitive annual balance sheet for 2026.
The press release does not indicate the precise day in January 2027 on which the new rate will take effect, nor does it describe changes for individual institutions or insured persons. Instead, it reports the scope of the decision, the indicators considered and the average degree of coverage. For institutional reference on social security, the [UFAS] page is available (https://www.bsv.admin.ch/it/telelavoro).
To learn more about pensions and LPP, pensione e LPP.
