item.title: AI reform: risk of asset depletion in 2031
item.description: The Federal Council put the next reform of disability insurance (DI) out for consultation on Wednesday.
item.content:encoded:
## TL;DR - AI risks depleting the assets by 2031 - New benefit for young people aged 18 to 24 - Liquidity and investments: 33% versus the legal 50% - Consultation deadline: 4 February 2027
## Key facts - Goal → professional integration and disability insurance finances - New benefit → approximately 1'000 francs per month - 2025 deficit → more than 200 million francs - Threshold for a full pension → from 70% to 80% - 2030 scenario → more than 600 million annual deficit
On Wednesday, the Federal Council put the next reform of disability insurance (DI) out for consultation. The project aims to strengthen professional integration and stabilize the insurance’s finances, with particular attention to new pensions granted to young adults with mental illnesses.
The deadline set for the consultation is 4 February 2027. The reform is not presented as sufficient on its own: the executive considers it necessary to also intervene on payroll contributions in order to permanently put DI on a sound financial footing.
In recent years, the number of people receiving a new DI pension has increased in all age groups. The increase is particularly problematic among 18- to 24-year-olds: many of these people face serious difficulties re-entering professional life or entering the workforce later on. For this reason, according to the Government, they may need a DI pension for a long time. The main reason cited for the increase among young adults is mental illness, a trend also observed in other countries.
### A benefit to support young people
The main proposed measure is a new benefit for young people between 18 and 24 who, because of their health conditions, cannot participate in DI professional integration measures but retain integration potential. The Federal Council estimates that this concerns approximately 1'000 people, or about one-third of the new pensions granted in this age group.
The aim is to provide young people with intensive and prolonged counselling and support, helping them better manage difficulties related to their illness and gradually approach the professional integration process. The benefit would include a monthly allowance of approximately 1'000 francs for integration, as well as individual and regular counselling from the DI office, with the involvement of the person’s social environment.
Financially, the situation remains critical. DI has had a structural deficit since the beginning of the 1990s. In 2025, the pay-as-you-go deficit exceeded 200 million francs; in the baseline scenario, the annual deficit could exceed 600 million by 2030. In addition, there is approximately 200 million in annual interest on the debt owed to AVS. Without countermeasures, the executive warns, DI’s assets would be completely depleted in 2031. ## The relationship between deficits and savings
The figures from the source become easier to read if they are separated by year and by type of amount. The pay-as-you-go deficit measures the imbalance indicated for the insurance scheme; interest, on the other hand, represents the annual cost of the AI's debt to the AVS. The savings cited by the Federal Council are an estimate of the effect of the proposed measures.
| Indicator | Value | Period | |---|---:|---| | Pay-as-you-go deficit | over 200 million francs | 2025 | | Annual deficit in the baseline scenario | over 600 million francs | 2030 | | Estimated savings from the measures | 150 million francs | 2030 | | Estimated savings from the measures | approximately 400 million francs | 2040 | | Interest on debt owed to the AVS | approximately 200 million francs a year | every year |
The most direct comparison concerns 2030: the estimated savings of 150 million francs are lower than the annual deficit which, in the baseline scenario, could exceed 600 million. This is the relationship indicated by the Government to explain why cuts in expenditure, although rising to approximately 400 million in 2040, would not on their own be sufficient to stabilize the insurance scheme over the long term and guarantee the necessary liquidity.
### The gap from the prescribed level
The situation of the AI Compensation Fund also shows a measurable difference. Currently, liquidity and investments amount to 33% of one year's expenditure of the insurance scheme, while the level prescribed by law is 50%. The arithmetic distance between the two values is 17 percentage points. The 33% therefore concerns the fund's financial resources relative to annual expenditure, not the share of new pensions among young people.
The source links this level to the fund's rapid depletion and warns that, without countermeasures, its assets would be exhausted in 2031. This is a time horizon indicated in the scenario described by the Federal Council, not a result that has already occurred.
### Two lines for integration
The reform supplements the benefit for young people with measures concerning training and continuing education. Currently, many young people, people with few qualifications or insured persons with low incomes do not meet the requirements for vocational reintegration. The project provides for better support and pathways more geared to the needs of the labor market, aiming to strengthen the prospects for lasting integration into the primary labor market.
The monthly benefit and regular counselling, by contrast, address the situation of those who cannot yet participate in the AI's vocational measures, despite having integration potential. Comparing the two measures shows that the proposal is not limited to modifying pensions: it combines prolonged support for a specific group with broader access to training. ## The measures envisaged and outstanding issues
In February 2026, the Federal Council tasked the Federal Department of Home Affairs with examining every possible measure to avert additional financing for Disability Insurance. The reform submitted for consultation therefore contains both expenditure-side measures and new revenues, some time-limited and others permanent.
The DI offices would be expected to contribute to easing the financial burden through organizational measures. To qualify for a full DI pension, the required degree of disability would rise from 70% to 80%; in addition, the daily allowance for people without maintenance obligations would be reduced, following a model similar to that of unemployment insurance.
### Savings and contributions
Overall, the Government estimates that these measures would reduce DI expenditure by 150 million francs in 2030. Thereafter, the savings would increase to approximately 400 million in 2040. The same source warns, however, that these amounts would not be sufficient to stabilize DI over the long term and ensure the necessary liquidity.
For this reason, the Federal Council considers it necessary to act on the revenue side as well. The government note indicates that, to put the insurance on a sustainable financial footing, payroll contributions would need to be increased by 0,2 percentage points. For the period from 2030 to 2039, it also proposes increasing the DI contribution rate by 0,05 percentage points. At the same time, the income compensation contribution rate would fall by the same amount.
The two figures serve different purposes in the text: 0,2% is presented as the increase needed for long-term financial stabilization, while 0,05% concerns a proposal limited to the period 2030-2039, offset by the reduction in the income compensation rate. The available passage ends after the reference to the OASI rates and does not provide enough information to describe other components of the financing.
### Training and wording of the law
The reform also affects the wording of the Federal Disability Insurance Act, referred to by the acronym LAI. The Federal Council proposes replacing individual terms that the people directly affected consider demeaning and outdated. The examples cited include German-language formulations containing the term «Invalide» to refer to certain people.
This part complements the measures on vocational integration: on the one hand, extended counselling for young people with integration potential; on the other, better access to training and continuing education. The source presents both measures as elements of the reform submitted for consultation, alongside the financial measures.
For the official reference on OASI and income compensation contributions, see the [OASI 2026 synoptic table](https://www.ahv-iv.ch/p/2.01.i). To learn more about pensions, consult rendite AVS/AI.

item.title: CDF criticizes Armasuisse Immobili for delays in renovations
item.description: Armasuisse Immobili is in fact unable to determine either the troops’ actual needs or the necessary investment with sufficient precision.
item.content:encoded:
## TL;DR - The CDF criticizes the management of Armasuisse Immobili - More than 34% of renovation costs at the end of 2025 - Backlog at 40% by 2030 according to internal projections - DDPS is aiming for a cap of 30 billion
## Key facts - Establishment → Swiss Federal Audit Office (SFAO) - Manager → Armasuisse Real Estate - Portfolio → around 21,600 objects, including 6,070 buildings - Replacement value → CHF 28.4 billion - Maintenance arrears → between CHF 2 billion and CHF 3 billion
### The contestation of the relationship The document published on Monday by the Swiss Federal Audit Office (SFAO) blames Armasuisse Real Estate for delays in the rehabilitation of military infrastructure and gaps in strategic planning. The criticism comes as new needs to strengthen the Swiss army put pressure on the management of real estate assets.
The portfolio includes barracks, airfields, parade grounds and logistics centres. At the end of 2025, it had around 21,600 objects, including 6,070 buildings, with an estimated new value of CHF 28.4 billion. This is the sum total of properties managed by Armasuisse Real Estate, not a single infrastructure.
The strategy on the base park changed in 2022. Previously, the goal was to reduce the value of the portfolio to CHF 20 billion; the deterioration of the geopolitical situation, on the other hand, led the Federal Department of Defence's (DDPS) Real Estate Council to target a ceiling of CHF 30 billion. According to the report, the changeover puts the management bodies under great pressure.
The expansion of the portfolio could require up to 6 billion francs. However, armasuisse Real Estate is unable to quantify the actual needs of the troops or to determine exactly how much investment is required. As for the planning documents of the Defence Group, including the future "Outlook 2040" report, they are not expected before the end of the year.
Petra Kobler, Head of Armasuisse Real Estate, acknowledged that catching up is not possible in the short term. Priorities will therefore have to be set. The SFAO welcomes the planned and partly already initiated portfolio management review because the errors identified have been corrected. Previously, it was often the individual site managers who defined the needs of users locally and with a short-term horizon. ## The backlog scale
### Three thresholds for reading the report The clearest comparison concerns renovation costs relative to the value of the real-estate portfolio. The report indicates a maximum target value of 25%. At the end of 2025, however, the share had risen above 34%, amounting to 7,3 billion francs. The gap between the target limit and the observed figure is therefore more than 9 percentage points.
| Threshold | Meaning indicated by the source | |---|---| | 25% | Maximum target value of renovation costs relative to the portfolio | | Above 34% | Share reached at the end of 2025, amounting to 7,3 billion francs | | 40% | Level projected by 2030 according to internal projections |
The three percentages measure the same item at different points in time: the limit set, the situation at the end of 2025, and the scenario indicated for 2030. The 40% therefore does not describe a figure already recorded. It is the projection of the “backlog wave” if investments are not doubled.
The report distinguishes this share from the maintenance backlog, which ranges between 2 and 3 billion francs. The two values are not presented as amounts to be added together: the first is a percentage of renovation costs relative to the portfolio, and the second is an estimate of accumulated maintenance work. This distinction makes it possible to avoid confusing the relative scale of the problem with the backlog amount indicated by the CDF.
### Portfolio and potential investments A second comparison concerns the evolution of the asset-portfolio target. The previous approach targeted a base portfolio of 20 billion francs, while the new maximum cap indicated by DDPS is 30 billion: a difference of 10 billion between the two strategic reference points. The source presents 30 billion as the maximum limit being pursued, not as a replacement value recorded at the end of 2025, which remains stated at 28,4 billion.
The 6 billion envisaged for expanding the portfolio must also remain separate from the 7,3 billion associated with renovation costs at the end of 2025. The report does not provide a definitive overall figure for the two categories. Armasuisse Immobili is in fact unable to determine either the troops’ actual needs or the necessary investment with sufficient precision. The forthcoming “2040 Outlook” report is expected no earlier than the end of the year, leaving the quantification of real-estate needs still open. ## Controls, governance and corrective measures underway
### An error in recent financial statements The problems do not concern maintenance alone. According to the Swiss Federal Audit Office, Armasuisse Immobili’s management control is based on Excel spreadsheets that contain contradictions and methodological flaws. An incorrect formula left maintenance expenditure of almost 250 million francs out of the most recent financial statements.
The figure concerns the quality of the control tools and the accounting presentation of expenditure. It adds to the problem of the backlog, but the source treats the formula error and the share of remediation costs separately. The report thus identifies two distinct dimensions: on the one hand, the accumulation of necessary work, and on the other, the reliability of the data used to monitor management.
### The gap in strategic decision-making From a governance perspective, the last two regular meetings of the DDPS Real Estate Council, a body bringing together senior management, were cancelled between the end of last year and the beginning of this year. This cancellation blocked any significant arbitration and fueled differences between the Armed Forces Group and Armasuisse.
The military side is pressing to relax certain environmental or legal constraints in order to free up resources for armaments. Civilian management, however, cannot endorse this practice without clear legal backing from senior leadership. The report therefore also links the planning problem to the lack of a decision-making level capable of resolving these differences.
### Coordination between real estate and armaments Armasuisse and the DDPS are implementing structural measures to make project direction and management more effective. One objective is to bring real estate and armament projects under unified leadership.
> «Interdependencies must be taken into account: for example, a new weapons system requires a dedicated hangar», Robert Scheidegger, Deputy Secretary General of the DDPS, explained to the media.
For Petra Kobler, the real estate portfolio must be systematically geared towards defence capability, giving priority to security needs over architectural and urban-planning considerations. The Swiss Federal Audit Office has issued four recommendations, including timely decisions in principle on governance, the immediate correction of accounting data and the mandatory adoption of modular construction standards.
The conclusions of the report were welcomed by the DDPS, Armasuisse and Army Command. The same parties stated that they had already overcome some coordination difficulties and had begun updating procedures. The source does not yet provide a definitive quantification of the investments required or indicate when the planning delay can be made up.
*Source: [rsi.ch](https://www.rsi.ch/s/4212855)*

item.title: 13th AVS pension: VAT increase put to a vote on November 29
item.description: On November 29, voters will vote on the implementation of the measure introducing the 13th AVS pension payment.
item.content:encoded:
## TL;DR - On November 29, there will be a vote on financing the 13th AHV pension - The standard VAT rate would rise from 8,1% to 8,5% - The accommodation rate would rise from 3,8% to 4% - The first 13th AHV pension will be paid in December
## Key facts - Vote → November 29 - Measure → 13th AVS pension payment - Initial support → over 58% of voters - Standard VAT → from 8,1% to 8,5% - Reduced VAT → 2,6%, unchanged
On November 29, voters will vote on the implementation of the measure introducing the 13th AVS pension payment. The vote comes two years after the vote that approved it with a clear double majority: over 58% of voters voted in favor.
### From the vote to the funding After the measure was approved, the issue of funding arose immediately. The initiative did not specify how to cover the new expenditure, but at the time of the vote it was already estimated that it would entail an additional outlay of approximately 4,1 billion francs per year. The source also notes that this amount was expected to grow rapidly.
The debate unfolded between the Federal Council and Parliament, with a lengthy and at times heated discussion. There were essentially two options: an increase in value-added tax supported by the Federal Council, or a mixed solution consisting of an increase in VAT and higher equal employer and employee payroll contributions for AVS.
After a couple of years of debate, the situation was resolved last June in favor of the first solution. Parliament accepted an indefinite increase in VAT. Since the measure requires a constitutional amendment, the final say will nevertheless rest with the people.
The timetable makes the decision imminent: the first 13th AVS payment will be paid to beneficiaries as early as December. The solution approved by the Chambers provides for an increase of 0,4 percentage points in the standard rate, from 8,1% to 8,5%. The special rate applied to the hotel sector would instead rise from 3,8% to 4%.
The reduced rate of 2,6%, applied to various everyday goods, including food and medicines, as well as to certain services in agriculture, would remain unchanged. According to the estimates reported by the source, the entire measure would entail an average additional burden of approximately 180 francs per household per year. ### Three rates, three treatments
The proposed structure clearly distinguishes the three VAT rates involved in financing the 13th AHV pension:
| Rate | Indicated level | Planned treatment | |---|---:|---| | Standard | 8,1% | Increase to 8,5% | | Special rate for accommodation | 3,8% | Increase to 4% | | Reduced | 2,6% | No increase |
The comparison shows that the proposal does not apply the same increase to all rates. The increase concerns the standard rate and the special rate for the accommodation sector, while the reduced rate remains at 2,6%. The source associates the latter with everyday goods such as food and medicines and with certain agricultural services. The decision not to change it is also presented by the Federal Council and Parliament as an element of social fairness.
For households, the quantitative reference is an average additional burden of around 180 francs per year. The figure is expressed as an average: it is therefore not presented as an identical amount for every household. The source does not provide an individual calculation based on actual consumption, but describes the general criterion according to which the proposal would distribute the additional revenue.
### Why VAT divides the political camps
The criticism stems from the very nature of the tax. As an indirect tax, VAT affects everyone through the same rates, regardless of income level or purchasing power. This is the point on which objections to financing the 13th AHV pension focus.
In the bourgeois camp, the consequences for household budgets are given priority. The solution proposed by opponents would not be another increase in VAT, but a combination of structural reforms and state budget priorities. On the left, by contrast, the shift in the tax burden toward consumption is emphasized, as is the greater burden that a tax such as VAT can place on people with limited means.
A minority had already opposed the proposal during the parliamentary debate. Its position was that expenditure related to the 13th AHV pension should be addressed within the framework of the next AHV reform, rather than financing the measure through an increase in value-added tax.
The Federal Council and Parliament, by contrast, defend the solution approved by the Chambers as a balanced measure. The stated rationale is the need to preserve the stability of AHV finances for future generations as well. Under this approach, the impact on people with medium or low incomes would be minimized, while those with higher incomes who consume more would contribute more to the additional VAT revenue. ### Estimates on revenues, deficits and reserves
VAT financing is also assessed in relation to the development of the AHV accounts. It is estimated that from 2029 the higher levies could bring in just under 1.5 billion francs in additional revenue to the first pillar. The source points out that this contribution would help to reduce the impact of the payment of the 13th pension.
The most detailed comparison concerns 2035. Taking into account the additional funding, the AHV deficit is estimated at around CHF 3 billion, compared to CHF 5 billion in the other scenario. The gap between the two values is therefore around CHF 2 billion for that year. This is a report calculated on the values reported from the source, not a new forecast.
Reserves from the first pillar are also used as an indicator. For 2035, estimates place them at around 70% of annual insurance expenditure, compared to around 50% in the other scenario. The comparison indicates a difference of 20 percentage points between the two scenarios described, again based on the estimates reported.
### A situation already under pressure
The source places these numbers within an already difficult financial framework. In the current year, AHV expenditures would be more than one billion francs higher than revenues. In addition, already the following year, the level of reserves would fall below the legal threshold of 100% of the insurance year's expenditure.
The payment of the 13th would have a further impact on a situation described as anything but reassuring. For this reason, the financing is not only presented as a question of revenue, but also as a measure linked to the deficit and the size of the AHV reserves.
The source does not quantify the additional cost per individual taxpayer, nor does it offer a distribution of the burden between different consumption or income groups. It also does not provide detailed amounts for the alternative based on wage contributions. The available data therefore make it possible to compare rates, the average burden per household and estimates on AHV accounts, but not to derive a personal figure for each voter or beneficiary.
For an official reference on pension provision, please refer to the [AHV 2026 Synoptic Table](https://www.ahv-iv.ch/p/2.01.i). To learn more about pensions, please refer to consulta la pensione AVS.

item.title: Swissport Zurich: failed negotiations for staff
item.description: Negotiations for a new collective bargaining agreement for Swissport’s ground staff in Zurich have failed, according to the unions.
item.content:encoded:
## TL;DR - CCL Swissport in Zurich: negotiations fail - The contract concerns approximately 2’000 people - Salary increases of up to 7% requested - Possible strike as early as January 2027
## Key facts - Subject → new collective bargaining agreement for ground staff - Location → Zurich - People involved → approximately 2’000 - Last renewal → 2022 - Expiry → end of the year - Salary demand → increases of up to 7% - Possible mobilization → strike possibly as early as January 2027
Negotiations for a new collective bargaining agreement for Swissport’s ground staff in Zurich have failed, according to the unions. The agreement covers approximately 2’000 people and will expire at the end of the year. The last renewal dates back to 2022; the unions maintain that, on that occasion, the covid pandemic had forced employees to accept numerous concessions.
### A breakdown that does not end the talks
The dispute nevertheless has two distinct elements. On the one hand, the unions describe the negotiations for the new CBA as having failed. On the other, they say they remain open to discussions. The strike threat is tied to an explicit condition: the demands must not be heeded. The source identifies January 2027 as a possible time for the action, not a strike that has already been decided.
The demands concern better working conditions and salary increases of up to 7 percent. The text does not present 7 percent as an achieved result, but as the upper limit of the unions’ demand. For the employees involved, the documented progression is therefore from failed negotiations to a phase in which a strike is being threatened, while a willingness to discuss remains indicated. ## From renewal to possible protest
Comparing the dates contained in the report makes it possible to read the dispute as a sequence, without turning the hypotheses into a definite schedule. 2022 is the last year indicated for the renewal; the end of the year is the date indicated for the contract’s expiry; January 2027, on the other hand, is the date mentioned as the possible start of a strike. The three indications therefore carry different weight: one concerns a past event, one the expiry of the CCL, and one an action that remains hypothetical.
| Time | Related element | |---|---| | 2022 | Last renewal of the contract | | End of the year | Expiry of the ground staff contract | | January 2027 | Possible strike threatened by the unions | | Four years ago | Protest actions had already taken place |
### The difference between the demand and the outcome
The wage figure should also be viewed with the same caution. The unions are calling for increases of up to 7 percent: the wording indicates a demand, not an increase that has already been agreed. The source does not provide a different percentage for individual categories, nor does it describe a partial agreement. For this reason, the possible comparison is not between 7 percent and a new actual wage, but between the content of the demand and the state of the negotiations.
The scope of the dispute is defined by the contract for ground staff and the figure of approximately 2’000 people. The number is presented as approximate, while no further details are provided about the composition of the workforce. The report thus makes it possible to distinguish what has already happened, what is nearing expiry and what could happen, without attributing an unreported outcome to the strike threat. ## What remains to be clarified
The source documents the unions' position, but does not report a response from Swissport to the demands. Nor does it indicate how the possible salary increase of up to 7 percent would be structured: it is not specified how the request would be distributed among workers, nor what the actual increase would be. These elements cannot be inferred from the reference to the maximum percentage alone.
### The precedent of the protests
The text notes that protest actions had already taken place four years ago. This places an earlier mobilization in the history of the dispute, but does not specify its form, duration, number of participants, or outcome. It therefore does not make it possible to establish a direct relationship between those actions and the current failure of the negotiations. Likewise, the threat of a strike does not, in the wording reported, amount to confirmation of a date: the unions speak of possible recourse to a strike, perhaps as early as January 2027, while at the same time stating that they intend to continue discussions.
The documented picture ends with these elements. The wording of the new contract, any response from Swissport, the actual percentage increase, and the outcome of the negotiations remain unspecified. The report therefore describes a negotiating phase accompanied by a threat of a strike, not a concluded agreement or an action that has already taken place.

item.title: October inflation rises to 1,5%, driven by energy
item.description: October’s annual inflation rose by 1.5% In September, the annual increase was 1% Monthly CPI increased by 0.2% Energy: diesel fuel, gasoline
item.content:encoded:
## TL;DR - Annual inflation in October rose by 1,5% - In September, the annual increase was 1% - The monthly CPI grew by 0,2% - Energy: heating oil, gasoline and diesel drove prices
## Key facts - Period → October - Annual inflation → 1,5% (September: 1%) - Monthly CPI → 0,2% - Economists' forecasts → between 1,1% and 1,4% - Main drivers → heating oil, petrol and diesel - Petroleum products → 2,1% of the basket; almost 85% of the monthly increase - Heating oil → +81,4% year on year - Imported products → +1,2% compared with September; +3,7% compared with October 2025
### The October figure
In October, inflation in Switzerland accelerated. According to the Federal Statistical Office (UST/BFS), the year-on-year change rose to 1,5%, while in September it was +1%. The consumer price index, or CPI, recorded an increase of 0,2% compared with the previous month. The two percentages therefore describe two different comparisons reported for the same month: the first year on year, the second with the previous month. The source explicitly presents the two results, distinguishing the annual change from the monthly one.
Economists' estimates for October inflation were between 1,1% and 1,4%; the actual figure, at 1,5%, exceeded the upper end of the range.
The movement in prices was mainly linked to increases in heating oil, petrol and diesel. For the cost of living, the figure provides an initial picture of the CPI, but the source points out that the weight in the basket and the contribution to the increase do not coincide. Petroleum products account for 2,1% of the consumption basket and explain almost 85% of the monthly increase in the index.
The figures should be read as changes in the index, not as an identical increase in every good: the same source in fact reports more moderate rises and declines in some categories, as well as different dynamics between imported and domestic products. The available snapshot is that of the October CPI, not an estimate of the price of every individual purchase. ### The weight of energy items
The relationship between the weight of petroleum products in the basket and their contribution to the monthly increase clarifies the structure of the October figure. The share indicated in the source is 2,1% of the consumer basket, while the contribution attributed to the rise in the index is almost 85%.
> Arthur Jurus, of financial group ODDO BHF, notes: “Petroleum products, which account for only 2,1% of the consumer basket, alone explain almost 85% of the monthly increase in the index”.
The comparison must be made over the correct periods: 2,1% describes the weight of the products in the basket, while 85% concerns the monthly increase in the index. The reported relationship does not say that every item followed the same trend; rather, it shows how concentrated the monthly movement was in these products.
| Item | Year-on-year change | |---|---:| | Heating oil | +81,4% | | Gasoline | +26,5% | | Diesel | +36,9% |
Heating oil therefore increased by 81,4% year on year. For gasoline, annual growth was 26,5%, while for diesel it reached 36,9%. These are the three values reported by the source for the main energy items, without turning them into a forecast of how prices will evolve.
The economist emphasizes that this winter households that heat with heating oil, as well as those that depend on a car daily, could find themselves facing a particularly costly energy bill. This is a possibility, not a cost already quantified for each household.
According to Jurus, price acceleration is linked above all to energy, not to an overheating of the Swiss economy. Consequently, the country is not experiencing generalized inflation, but rather a concentrated energy shock, with very unequal effects among households. The same national figure can therefore affect citizens’ wallets differently. ### Increases and decreases in the other categories
The monthly movement in the CPI also includes non-energy items. The source reports that women's footwear prices increased by 10,5% and men's footwear prices by 8,6%. In the same comparison, outpatient medical services at hospitals recorded an increase of 1,1%. The source describes these increases as more moderate than those in the items that drove the index.
By contrast, prices for medical services at doctors' offices (−3%), international package tours (−2,5%) and the hotel sector (−2,9%) decreased. The sign of the change is essential: these three figures describe month-on-month declines, not increases.
The year-on-year comparison also shows changes in different sectors. Car rental and car sharing recorded an increase of 11,5%, while personal computers rose by 11%. The source does not present these items as the main explanation for the surge; instead, it indicates that heating oil, petrol and diesel in particular drove prices higher.
The picture varies depending on the origin of the products: imported products increased by 1,2% compared with September and by 3,7% compared with October 2025, while domestic products recorded changes of −0,1% month on month and −0,8% year on year. For imported products, the monthly comparison is therefore with September, and the annual comparison with October 2025.
The text adds that the strong franc helps to cushion the shock, while rising prices are mainly those of products from abroad. No breakdown by cantons or individual households is provided: the available figure therefore remains that of the Swiss CPI and does not make it possible to measure the spending of each household. For more details, see cost of living in Switzerland.

item.title: Labor market outlook: slight weakening in the fourth quarter of 2026
item.description: The score of 2,0 points recorded for the fourth quarter of 2026 signals a slight weakening in employment prospects in Switzerland.
item.content:encoded:
## TL;DR - KOF indicator at 2,0 points in the fourth quarter of 2026 - It stood at 2,3 points in the previous quarter - Approximately 4'500 companies surveyed in October - Construction positive; food service and retail declining
## Key facts - KOF indicator → 2,0 points - Period → fourth quarter of 2026 - Previous period → 2,3 points - Multi-year average → 1,7 points - Companies surveyed → approximately 4'500 - Current staff → 0,8 points - Next three months → 3,2 points - Other services → 4,4 points
### The national figure The score of 2,0 points recorded for the fourth quarter of 2026 signals a slight weakening in employment prospects in Switzerland. However, the number of companies expecting to increase jobs remains higher than the number of companies anticipating a reduction.
The quarterly employment survey conducted by the KOF Institute of the Swiss Federal Institute of Technology Zurich (ETH) showed a decline compared with the 2,3 points recorded in the previous quarter, according to a statement published today. In October, approximately 4'500 companies were surveyed.
The overall result remains above the multi-year average of 1,7 points. According to KOF, this level points to solid employment growth in the coming months. The national picture therefore remains positive, although the comparison with the previous quarter shows a limited deterioration.
The indicator combines two assessments by companies. The first concerns current staff: companies indicate whether they employ too many or too few employees. The second concerns the following three months and measures the intention to hire or reduce staff.
The result is mainly affected by the less favourable assessment of current staff, whose specific indicator fell from 1,3 to 0,8 points. Companies that consider staffing insufficient nevertheless remain more numerous than those that consider it excessive. Expectations for the following three months remained almost stable: the indicator fell from 3,3 to 3,2 points. ## How the change is distributed
### The comparison between the components The KOF indicator is not based on a single question. It combines the assessment of the current workforce with companies' intentions for the following three months. This structure makes it possible to distinguish the assessment of staff already employed from short-term expectations.
| Item | Previous value | Current value | Arithmetic difference | |---|---:|---:|---:| | Overall indicator | 2,3 | 2,0 | -0,3 | | Assessment of the current workforce | 1,3 | 0,8 | -0,5 | | Expectations for the next three months | 3,3 | 3,2 | -0,1 |
The differences are calculated by subtracting the current value from the previous one: the overall indicator falls by 0,3 points, the current-workforce component by 0,5 and the future-intentions component by only 0,1. The comparison shows why KOF refers to a slight deterioration: the largest change concerns the current situation of companies, while plans for the short term change little.
Even after the decline, both components remain positive: 0,8 points for the workforce assessment and 3,2 points for expectations. The overall figure of 2,0 points is also 0,3 points above the multi-year average of 1,7. According to KOF, this gap remains compatible with a solid employment trend in the following months.
The survey therefore does not describe a single signal. On the one hand, companies are less positive when assessing the current number of employees. On the other hand, the component focused on the following three months remains almost stable. The source also specifies that companies whose workforce is considered insufficient are still more numerous than those that consider it excessive. The picture that emerges is therefore less favorable than in the previous quarter, but still positive overall. ## Sectors with opposing signals
### From construction to services The trend varies from one sector to another. In construction, companies expecting more jobs clearly outnumber the others; in the hotel and restaurant sector, as in retail, those anticipating a reduction prevail.
The so-called “other services” continue to represent an important pillar of Swiss employment. Their indicator stands at 4,4 points, therefore still clearly positive, but the picture has deteriorated: at the end of 2025 it reached 9,6 points and now stands at levels last observed at the beginning of 2021.
Wholesale and manufacturing, on the other hand, show signs of recovery compared with the end of 2025, when their indicators were still clearly below zero. Today, the former stands at -1,0 points and the latter at -3,4 points. Employment prospects therefore remain negative in both sectors, despite the improvement.
The combination of the data describes a labour market that is not uniform across sectors: construction and other services show positive signals, hotels, restaurants and retail show a prevalence of expectations of reduction, while wholesale and manufacturing are improving but remain below zero.
The source does not indicate the reasons for the sectoral differences and does not provide a breakdown by individual companies, geographical areas or Cantons. Nor does it quantify wages, unemployment or jobs actually created or lost. The available data concern companies’ assessments and expectations, not an already measured development in employment.
*Source: [swissinfo.ch](https://www.swissinfo.ch/ita/mercato-del-lavoro%3a-le-prospettive-si-offuscano-leggermente/92312143)*

item.title: 21,4 million francs for large hydroelectric plants
item.description: For the 2026 market premiums, relating to the 2025 financial year, the total amount is 21,4 million francs.
item.content:encoded:
## TL;DR - 21,4 million francs to three applicants - The 2026 premium relates to the 2025 financial year - Applications were submitted by the end of May 2026 - Available resources were not used in full
## Key facts - Date: November 2, 2026 - Location: Bern - Institution: UFE - Amount: 21,4 million francs - Applicants: three - Corresponding energy: 2142 million kilowatt-hours - Share: approximately 5,7 percent of national hydropower production in 2025 - Limit: 1 cent per kilowatt-hour
### The announcement from Bern On November 2, 2026, from Bern, the release states that the Energy Act currently in force allows operators and owners of large hydropower plants in Switzerland to request a market premium for the electricity they produce when they have been forced to sell it on the market at a price below production costs. The condition must be substantiated, and the entitlement arises when revenues do not cover production costs.
For the 2026 market premiums, relating to the 2025 financial year, the total amount is 21,4 million francs. The sum is paid to three applicants. The resources available for this instrument amount to approximately 100 million francs, but in 2026 they are not used in full. The figure therefore distinguishes the available allocation from the amount actually awarded for the applications examined.
By the end of May 2026, the annual deadline for submission, three applications had been received by the UFE, for a total amount of approximately 21,4 million francs. To assess them, the UFE compared the production costs of electricity with the revenues generated. The release specifies that the comparison serves to verify whether the costs are covered or whether revenues are lower than costs.
The production associated with the 2026 contribution is stated as 2142 million kilowatt-hours and represents a share of approximately 5,7 percent of national hydropower production in 2025. For the 2024 financial year, the preceding year, approximately 19,6 million francs had been paid to three applicants. The comparison is reported by the same communication, without attributing the difference between the two amounts to a specific cause.
Information on the beneficiaries is not published individually. Under Article 98 paragraph 4 of the Energy Promotion Ordinance, data relating to recipients of the market premium may be disclosed exclusively in aggregated form. The report therefore makes the amounts, number of applicants and corresponding production available, but not the identity of the individual recipients. ## How the premium is determined
### Comparing costs and revenues The calculation starts with a review by the SFOE. For each application, electricity production costs and the revenues generated are compared. Entitlement to the premium exists when production costs are not covered, that is, when revenues are lower than costs. The rule therefore links disbursement to a difference measured for the financial year in question.
When determining revenues, the SFOE takes several sales and remuneration channels into account. The comparison includes revenues from sales on the electricity exchange resulting from trading for the following day, the so-called day-ahead market, and revenues from system services. It also includes long-term electricity trading, referred to as the forward market, the winter reserve, and the sale of guarantees of origin.
The premium is capped at 1 cent per kilowatt-hour of energy produced, equivalent to 1,0 ct./kWh. The data reported for 2026 illustrate this limit in concrete terms: dividing the 21,4 million francs indicated by the 2142 million kilowatt-hours associated with the contribution, the ratio is 0,01 francs per kilowatt-hour, that is, 1 cent. The result matches the prescribed maximum, without changing the rule that the premium compensates only for uncovered production costs.
| Item | 2026 premium | 2024 financial year | |---|---:|---:| | Reference year | 2025 | 2024 | | Amount disbursed | 21,4 million francs | approximately 19,6 million francs | | Applicants | three | three |
The nominal difference between the amounts indicated for the two financial years is approximately 1,8 million francs. Since both figures are presented as approximate values, the comparison should be read as a difference between the reported amounts, not as a more precise measure of the funding requirement.
### Where the resources come from Around 100 million francs from the Grid Surcharge Fund are allocated to the market premium each year. The Fund is financed by the grid surcharge, which final consumers pay for each kilowatt-hour of electricity consumed. The grid surcharge is 2,3 ct./kWh.
Of the grid surcharge, 0,2 ct./kWh are allocated to the market premium. The Fund also finances other support instruments, including the feed-in remuneration system for electricity, one-off remunerations, and investment contributions for renewable energy. The availability of around 100 million francs and the actual disbursement of 21,4 million therefore describe two different quantities: the former concerns the annual resources planned for the instrument, while the latter concerns the applications funded in 2026. ## Duration and distinction from other instruments
### Affected facilities and deadlines Since 2018, the Energy Act has provided for the market premium as a support instrument for large domestic hydropower plants. The definition covers plants with a capacity above 10 MW. The benefit is granted to those bearing the risk that production costs remain uncovered: operators, owners or electricity supply companies.
To access the premium reserved for unprofitable large hydropower plants, applications must be submitted to the UFE no later than May 31 each year. The UFE is responsible for examining them, with the technical and administrative support of AFRY Schweiz AG. The May 31 deadline clarifies the ordinary deadline for the procedure, while the communication of November 2, 2026 reports the outcome of applications relating to the 2025 financial year.
The instrument has a limited duration. The final disbursement of the market premium will take place in 2031 and will refer to the 2030 financial year. The sequence indicated by the source therefore distinguishes the year of the financial year from the year in which the contribution is disbursed: the 2026 premiums concern 2025, while the final planned disbursement will be linked to 2030.
### The floating premium for new plants The premium intended for existing large hydropower plants is distinct from the floating market premium. The latter applies to new hydropower plants and those undergoing expansion or renovation.
Operators of hydropower plants can now choose whether to apply for a floating market premium or an investment contribution. Investment contributions have existed since 2018. Both instruments promote an increase in electricity production from renewable sources. For hydropower plants, the floating premium could first be applied for in June 2026.
The source also points to an information sheet on the 2026 market premium, published on November 2, 2026, with further information and prospects for the 2027 market premium. The materials mentioned also include a blog by Energeiaplus.com dated July 1, 2026. However, the communication keeps the information on beneficiaries aggregated, as provided for by Article 98 paragraph 4 of the Energy Promotion Ordinance: the names of individual applicants and an individual breakdown of 21,4 million francs are therefore not provided.
*Source: [admin.ch](https://www.admin.ch/it/newnsb/7g6Bepjb5CXM)*

item.title: Open Call 2026: training and funding for social startups
item.description: Startups with social and environmental impact can apply to Social Business Earth’s Open Call 2026 until January 15, 2027.
item.content:encoded:
## TL;DR - Applications open until 15 January 2027 - 20.000 francs up for grabs for five selected startups - Social Business Conference 2027 in Lugano on 19 May - Training, networking and personalized mentoring
## Key facts - What → Social Business Earth’s Open Call 2026 - Organizer → Social Business Earth - Deadline → January 15, 2027 - Prize → 20.000 francs for five enterprises - Event → Social Business Conference 2027 - Date and location → May 19, Lugano - Target audience → early-stage social and environmental startups - Requirements → at least six months old, no more than four years old, and initial traction
Startups with social and environmental impact can apply to Social Business Earth’s Open Call 2026 until January 15, 2027. The initiative offers them a support program, opportunities to expand their network of contacts, and the possibility of participating in the Sapiens Natura Prize.
The Open Call is Social Business Earth’s gateway to its support program. The organization promotes social entrepreneurship and the spread of sustainable business models aimed at producing positive effects on society and the environment. The 2026–2027 edition of the program will be carried out with the support of the Drosos Foundation in Zurich.
### From the program to the presentation
The selected enterprises will enter a training program focused on three areas: strengthening the business model, developing the business strategy, and measuring the impact generated. The program is therefore not limited to the initial presentation of the project, but supports the admitted ventures in defining their activities and evaluating the results produced.
The program will culminate in the Social Business Conference 2027, scheduled for May 19 in Lugano. There, the startups will be able to present their projects with a pitch in front of potential investors and key stakeholders.
The Sapiens Natura Prize will also be awarded during the conference. The total prize pool is 20.000 francs and will be distributed among five enterprises: 10.000 francs to the first-place finisher, 5.000 to the second, 3.000 to the third, and 1.000 francs each to the fourth and fifth. In addition to the financial award, all five winning enterprises will be able to access a personalized mentoring program, with international experts tasked with addressing the specific challenges of the individual ventures and strengthening their growth prospects. ## A multi-level prize
The structure of the initiative combines two distinct but connected elements: a support programme for the selected businesses and a prize awarded at the end of the programme. The training covers the business model, strategy and impact measurement; the financial award, on the other hand, is presented during the Social Business Conference 2027 in Lugano, after the projects have been presented through a pitch.
### The distribution of the 20.000 francs
The amounts indicated for the five positions show precisely how the overall prize pool is distributed.
| Position | Amount | Share calculated on 20.000 francs | |---|---:|---:| | First place | 10.000 francs | 50% | | Second place | 5.000 francs | 25% | | Third place | 3.000 francs | 15% | | Fourth place | 1.000 francs | 5% | | Fifth place | 1.000 francs | 5% |
The calculation shows that the first three positions collectively receive 18.000 francs, that is, 90% of the total. The remaining share, amounting to 2.000 francs, is divided equally between fourth and fifth place. The percentages derive exclusively from the amounts stated for the prize and the total of 20.000 francs.
The financial allocation is not the full extent of the support provided. The text also provides personalized mentoring to the five winning businesses, without differentiating the benefit according to the position achieved. The international experts will have to address the specific challenges of each business and help strengthen its growth prospects.
The sequence described therefore distinguishes between access to the programme, the training activities and the final presentation and award phase. The Open Call constitutes the first step; support and training then follow for the selected businesses, while the prize and mentoring concern the five winning businesses identified by the initiative. ## Who the Open Call is for
The scope of the application is defined by the impact that the startup intends to create. Entrepreneurial ventures that contribute to the Sustainable Development Goals of the United Nations 2030 Agenda may participate.
### Social impact and environmental sustainability
The source identifies two main directions. The first concerns improving people's quality of life, with particular attention to those in disadvantaged situations. The second concerns the development of innovative solutions for environmental sustainability. The thematic requirement is therefore not linked to a single sector: the text links eligibility to the contribution to the Sustainable Development Goals and to the nature of the impact pursued.
The Open Call is intended in particular for early-stage startups. At least six months of operations and an establishment date no more than four years ago are required. Companies must also have already demonstrated initial traction, measurable in terms of users, customers or revenue. These three indicators are the ones explicitly identified to describe the initial response generated by the activity.
The available material does not specify the number of startups that will enter the program, the selection schedule or the criteria according to which applications will be evaluated. Nor does it provide a list of eligible sectors beyond the two areas of social and environmental impact described. The required stage of development, the minimum duration of operations and the need for initial traction are, however, clear.
To access the Open Call 2026, applications must be submitted by 15 January 2027 via the form available on the official Social Business Earth website. The program reserved for selected ventures is linked to the Social Business Conference 2027, scheduled for 19 May in Lugano, where the projects will be presented and the Sapiens Natura Prize awarded.

item.title: Modernizers vs. conservatives: Act II in the tax battle over couples
item.description: The story is presented as Act II of the clash between "modernizers" and "conservatives".
item.content:encoded:
## TL;DR - March 8 is presented as a “revolution” under threat - The model identified as a threat is income pooling - The source refers to the second act of the tax dispute
## Key facts - Theme → taxation of couples - Voting → in the centre of Act II - Deployments evoked → "modernizers" and "conservatives" - Time reference → 8 March
March 8 is the reference around which the source describes a new passage of the comparison on the taxation of couples. The text defines that date as a "revolution" and argues that it is in danger, indicating in the income accumulation model the threat at the center of the discussion.
The story is presented as Act II of the clash between "modernizers" and "conservatives". The available material talks about a vote and describes it as an appointment with the smell of revenge, but does not report either the result or a complete date of the consultation. It does not even indicate the year related to March 8.
### The lexicon used by the source
The words chosen define the political tone of the confrontation, not an official map of the sides. The source does not associate the "modernizers" and "conservatives" with specific parties, parliamentarians, associations or cantons. For this reason, it is possible to report the contrast as it is presented, without attributing positions to subjects who are not named in the text.
The central figure remains the accumulation of income, cited as a model that threatens the "revolution" of March 8. However, the text does not explain its technical operation, does not indicate rates, deductions, thresholds or categories of couples concerned. The article can therefore reconstruct the perimeter of the debate, but not transform the description of the source into a calculation on the tax due or a judgment on the outcome of the vote.
What emerges is a national tax comparison presented as a rematch. Everything else must remain limited to the information actually reported. ## Three tax levels to keep distinct
To understand the issue without attributing details that are not present, it is useful to separate the political debate from the structure of taxation. The verified tax reference distinguishes three levels: direct federal tax, cantonal tax and municipal tax. Each canton has its own law and its own multiplier; the municipality applies a multiplier to the cantonal tax.
This structure provides a concrete comparison with the source text. The article identifies the political issue, namely the taxation of couples, and indicates income pooling as the contested model. It does not, however, specify whether the vote concerns direct federal tax, the cantonal level, the municipal level or several levels at once. It is therefore not possible to link the vote to a tax rate, a canton or a specific administration.
| Element | Available information | Limitation of the material | |---|---|---| | Topic | Taxation of couples | No regulatory details | | Model | Income pooling | No numerical effect indicated | | Tax structure | Federal, cantonal and municipal levels | No explicit connection with the vote | | Consultation | Vote described as act II | No result reported |
### Comparison between the headline and verifiable data
The headline sets up a political opposition: “modernizers” versus “conservatives”. The verified tax framework, by contrast, is administrative and distinguishes between the levels of taxation. These are two different dimensions. The first describes the confrontation as it is recounted by the source; the second clarifies that the term taxation does not by itself identify a single tax item.
The distinction is relevant to avoid confusing the income-pooling model with a measure that has already been quantified. The material contains no amounts, percentages, changes in the tax burden or comparison periods. Consequently, it is possible to explain where the issue fits within the Swiss tax system, but not to calculate who would pay more or less. The text allows a connection between the debate about couples and the three tax levels; however, it does not document which level would be changed by the vote. ## The scope of the available facts
The source makes it possible to identify the subject and tone of the dispute, but not to reconstruct in detail the proposal put to the vote. It does not indicate the text of the measure, the authority that submitted it, the parties involved, the cantons concerned, the full date of the vote or its outcome. It also lacks figures that would make it possible to compare the tax treatment before and after the income aggregation model.
### Expressions are not an outcome
The word «revolution» referring to March 8 and the expression «with an air of revenge» belong to the source’s journalistic description. They signal the importance attributed to the confrontation, but do not prove the approval or rejection of a measure. Likewise, «modernizers» and «conservatives» are the labels used in the title: the material provides no names or statements that would make it possible to turn them into formally defined factions.
Some passages that would be necessary to discuss concrete effects therefore remain excluded. It cannot be claimed that income aggregation increases or reduces a couple’s tax, or that it produces a change in federal direct tax, cantonal tax or municipal tax. The reference to the three levels of taxation describes the general structure established, not the outcome of the vote recounted by the source.
Nor is the reference to March 8 sufficient to construct a complete chronology. The text does not specify whether that date coincides with the consultation, with a previous decision or with the moment defined as a «revolution». The most faithful reconstruction therefore remains limited to the facts presented: a vote on the taxation of couples, income aggregation described as a threat, and a second act in the confrontation between «modernizers» and «conservatives». Any further detail would require information that does not appear in the material provided.

item.title: Over 30 tools for future climate risks in Switzerland
item.description: More than 30 products have been developed as part of NCCS-Impacts, the National Centre for Climate Services programme launched in 2022 and now coming
item.content:encoded:
## TL;DR - More than 30 tools for future climate risks - NCCS-Impacts started in 2022 - Five projects, more than 100 people involved - About 9 million francs allocated
## Key facts - Programme → NCCS-Impacts - Launch → 2022 - Products → more than 30 - Projects → 5 - People involved → more than 100 - Organizations → more than 20 - Funding → approximately 9 million francs - Presentation → October 29, third Swiss Climate Forum
More than 30 products have been developed as part of NCCS-Impacts, the National Centre for Climate Services programme launched in 2022 and now coming to an end. Scenarios, models and digital tools were developed to assess the effects of climate change on forests, agriculture, water and health.
The project aims to enable policymakers, public administrations, the economy and society to identify climate risks at an early stage and take them into account in planning. It thus brought together scientific knowledge and applications for various areas of life in Switzerland, without focusing on a single sector.
### A programme of the federal legislative period
The programme brought together non-governmental organizations, companies, research institutes and Federal Offices, as well as other partners, with the task of examining the consequences of climate change, filling knowledge gaps and developing solutions that could be used in practice.
The Confederation reports that collaboration between public administration, the scientific community and practitioners made it possible to gain a deeper understanding of the effects of climate change on ecosystems, infrastructure, the economy and health. The same work also addressed possible options for action.
Christian Hofer, who chairs the NCCS Directors’ Conference and heads the Federal Office for Agriculture, summarizes the programme’s starting point as follows: “Effective adaptation to climate change requires reliable basic knowledge.” According to Hofer, the new knowledge has been transformed into concrete tools to better manage the consequences of climate change and lay the foundations for a resilient Switzerland. ## From climate risks to sector-specific tools
### A framework spanning multiple sectors
The program’s central characteristic is the breadth of the sectors analyzed. The source describes new socioeconomic scenarios together with digital applications that make it possible to move from general risk assessment to assessments relating to forests, agriculture, water and health.
| Area | Analysis or application indicated in the source | |---|---| | Forests | Identify tree species suited to a given habitat | | Agriculture | Estimate agricultural yields | | Water | Analyze nutrient loads | | Health | Manage hospital admissions and represent the risk of urban heat islands |
The comparison between these tools shows a plurality of uses. For forests, the result concerns the compatibility between tree species and habitats. For agriculture, the focus is on yields. In the water sector, by contrast, the application considers nutrient loads; in healthcare, the solutions include a tool for managing hospital admissions and maps dedicated to the risk associated with urban heat islands.
In Switzerland, the effects of warming are already tangible: the various heatwaves, record temperatures and marked drought of the record-breaking summer of 2026 highlighted the simultaneous impact on multiple sectors.
Falling river and lake levels, together with high temperatures, affected water resources and navigation. During the same period, agriculture and forests suffered from drought, while the heatwave put people and animals under severe strain. The program therefore uses tools targeting different phenomena, which the Confederation considers part of a cross-sectoral framework.
Another result concerns the quantification, for the first time, of the costs of certain climate risks and the related adaptation measures. This wording is limited to certain risks and measures: the source does not present an overall cost of climate change for Switzerland, but points to a method for measuring certain components.
These elements explain the relationship between scientific scenarios, planning and decision-making. The applications are not presented solely as collections of data: according to the Confederation, they should help policymakers, public administrations, the economy and society recognize risks in a timely manner and develop targeted adaptation measures. ## Funding, collaboration and dissemination of results
### A network between administration and research
A total of approximately 9 million francs was made available for the five projects and coordination.
More than 100 people from over 20 organizations took part in the work. The programme therefore brought together public administration, scientific institutes, businesses, non-governmental organizations and other partners. The Confederation attributes to this collaboration a deeper understanding of the effects of climate change on ecosystems, infrastructure, the economy and health, as well as an analysis of intervention options.
The NCCS-Impacts website brings together the results of the completed programme. The products will be presented on October 29 at the third Swiss Climate Forum, where they will be discussed with representatives of public administration, research, the economy and professional circles.
The forum thus constitutes the occasion identified by the source for presenting the applications and comparing them with practitioners in the relevant sectors. It is not described as a single project, but as the conclusion of a programme comprising five projects and more than 30 products, including scenarios, models and digital tools.
According to the Confederation, the body of knowledge gathered should help to better understand the effects of climate change, identify risks in good time and develop targeted adaptation measures. The need is linked above all to the increase in extreme weather events.
The source therefore presents the work carried out as a basis for decision-making in future planning. The results include applications for forests, agriculture, water and health, a quantification of the costs of certain risks, and tools for dealing with periods of heat. Their stated function is to support more informed decisions by institutions, the economy and Swiss society.

item.title: Medicines: mandatory stockpiles under pressure in Switzerland
item.description: There has been a shortage of antibiotics and painkillers in Switzerland for years.
item.content:encoded:
## TL;DR - Switzerland has been short of antibiotics and painkillers for years. - Since 2022, stocks have been released more than 100 times a year. - Reserves, costs and supply were discussed in Burgdorf. - Producers of active ingredients are concentrated in Asia.
## Key facts What → mandatory medicine reserves Where → Burgdorf 2018 → 17 releases of the reserves From 2022 → more than 100 releases per year Warehouse → as large as five football fields and 15 meters high Authorization → necessary for the mandatory reserve portion
### The debate and the reserves On Wednesday, in Burgdorf, the discussion also involved the people responsible for the mandatory reserves. The meeting served to describe the concrete situation, the challenges and the possible measures while Parliament examines the initiative «Yes to secure medical supply» together with the government counterproposal.
The starting point is the shortage of medicines, which has concerned Switzerland for years. The examples cited include antibiotics and painkillers. The warehouse described during the meeting stores millions of boxes of medicines; the facility occupies an area equivalent to five football fields and reaches 15 meters in height. A limited fraction of these packages constitutes the so-called mandatory reserves, that is, reserves intended to address situations of severe shortage.
Bernhard Megert, director of Alloga, explained the distinction between the packages available for the market and those subject to Confederation control:
> «Of 10’000 packages of a medicine present in the warehouse, 3’000 constitute the mandatory reserve: the other 7’000 can be freely placed on the market, while authorization from the Confederation is required for those reserved».
The example shows that the physical presence of medicines in storage does not mean that all packages have the same status. The portion not included in the mandatory reserve can be freely placed on the market; federal authorization is required for the restricted share.
In recent years, recourse to this authorization has become more frequent. In 2018, the mandatory reserves were released on 17 occasions; from 2022 onward, the threshold of 100 annual releases was exceeded every year. These figures, presented in Burgdorf, describe the growing pressure on the reserve system. ### The comparison between releases and costs The comparison first examines developments over time. In 2018, 17 releases of compulsory stocks were recorded; from 2022 onward, the figure exceeded 100 per year.
| Period | Number of releases | | --- | ---: | | 2018 | 17 | | From 2022 onward | more than 100 per year |
The comparison shows a much higher frequency than the 2018 figure, but does not provide the precise number for each subsequent year. Therefore, the source does not allow a detailed annual average or percentage increase to be calculated. The documented figure remains the increase from 17 releases in 2018 to a threshold above 100 in the years from 2022 onward.
For Peter Huber, the increase is attributable to the pandemic and armed conflicts. Huber chairs Helvecura, the cooperative responsible for coordinating the establishment of compulsory stocks. In his view, however, the reserves have always been sufficient. The data and this assessment therefore refer to two distinct aspects: the number of authorizations to release stocks and the adequacy of the available reserves.
The issue identified by Huber concerns financing. The comparison with other products makes the disparity contested by the sector clear:
| Products mentioned | Treatment of stock costs | | --- | --- | | Petrol, animal feed and food products | The costs are borne by consumers | | Medicines | Prices are regulated and the same mechanism is not possible |
For medicines, therefore, the sector does not accept that the costs of the reserves should be treated differently from those of petrol, animal feed or food products. The amount at stake is stated as a few million francs, without a more precise figure. Roland Pfister, Delegate for Economic Supply of the Country, said he understood the request. The Confederation is working to find a solution for financing the compulsory stocks. ### Dependence on Asia for older medicines The other issue concerns older medicines, those whose patents have expired. Urs B. Kientsch, a militia officer with the country's economic supply organization, identifies dependence on Asia as a separate issue from financing the reserves. Active ingredient manufacturers are concentrated there. The text therefore identifies the area where production is concentrated, but does not quantify the share of active ingredients involved.
The solution indicated by Kientsch is to encourage active ingredient manufacturers to return to Europe in order to supply the local market. For this to happen, in his assessment, policymakers must create favorable framework conditions. The source does not specify which conditions should be introduced, nor does it indicate any measure already decided or a timeline for the manufacturers' return.
There are also precise information gaps regarding financing. The amount is described only as a few million francs, and no breakdown of the costs is provided. Likewise, the figure for releases since 2022 is expressed as a threshold of more than 100 times a year, without the exact number for each year. There is therefore no basis for estimating a precise total for the period or comparing individual medicines.
The report also distinguishes between drug shortages and the availability of reserves: shortages have concerned Switzerland for years, while Huber states that the reserves have always been sufficient. The increase in authorizations is not presented as evidence that the stocks have been depleted. Rather, the documented discussion concerns how to finance them and dependence on foreign countries for certain medicines.
On the political level, Parliament is discussing the “Yes to Security of Medical Supply” initiative and the government's counterproposal. The Confederation says it is working on a solution for financing, but the text does not report a final decision. Both the economic issue of the reserves and the industrial issue linked to active ingredients concentrated in Asia therefore remain unresolved.

item.description: With the aim of reducing costs, Parliament had allocated a budget four years ago to finance the transformation of the database. However, estimates
item.content:encoded:
## TL;DR - SEM risks paralysis without additional resources - SIMIC: from approximately 66 million to an estimated 193 million in 2024 - The new system will not be operational before 2032 - Switzerland-EU package: requirements to be met by 2028
## Key facts - → SIMIC DATABASE - Users → 30,000 between Confederation, Cantons and Municipalities - Initial estimate → about 66 million - SEM estimate in 2024 → 193 million - Operations → no earlier than 2032
### The project and the relationship
In the report published on Monday evening, the Federal Financial Control warns that the State Secretariat for Migration (SEM) could be paralysed if it does not obtain additional resources to transform its database. The system in question is SIMIC, now outdated, which collects the data of foreign citizens residing in Switzerland.
With the aim of reducing costs, Parliament had allocated a budget four years ago to finance the transformation of the database. However, estimates have increased: in 2024 SEM revalued the cost of the renewal to 193 million, while the initial estimate amounted to about 66 million.
SIMIC has 30,000 users between the Confederation, Cantons and Municipalities. The data shows that the database involves the three levels of administration indicated in the report, without the source dividing the users among them or describing what operations they carry out through the system.
The report warns that the problem is not only about the transformation of the database: SEM's ability to guarantee its activities is also at risk. Comparing the reported figures requires keeping the estimate, the reassessment, and the outlook on delays distinct. The first point of reference is the budget of approximately 66 million allocated by Parliament four years ago. The second is the estimate of 193 million prepared by SEM in 2024. The report adds that the renewal should cost four times as much as initially planned. The source does not provide a breakdown of expenditure items and does not assign separate amounts to the Confederation, the cantons, or the municipalities.
### Three figures for understanding the project
| Item | Reported figure | |---|---| | Initial budget | approximately 66 million | | SEM estimate in 2024 | 193 million | | Additional costs in the event of delays | 25 million per year | | Operational status of the new system | no earlier than 2032 |
The 25 million figure is not a new total estimate for the renewal: the document presents it as an additional annual cost that could result from further delays. 2032 is also reported as a time limit: the new system will not be operational before that year. Distinguishing between the two pieces of information avoids confusing the cost of the project with the potential cost of postponing it.
The database also has a defined administrative scope: it collects data on foreign citizens residing in Switzerland and is used by 30'000 users across the Confederation, the cantons and the municipalities. The text does not specify how the transformation will change users' access, which functions will be transferred, or which services could be disrupted. The only explicitly stated effect is the risk to SEM's ability to carry out its activities. The report then shifts attention from the figures alone to SEM's organizational capacity. The agency will have to meet by 2028 the requirements arising from the Switzerland-EU package. To meet that deadline, the document states that the necessary human resources must be ensured with the utmost urgency. However, the text does not specify either the size of the staff or the individual activities included in those requirements.
### Funding and institutional response
As part of the 2027 relief plan, the Federal Council reduced funding to renew the system. The report points to further reductions planned for 2029 and 2030. In the document, these cuts are associated with the revision of the project requested by the Federal Audit Office, which considers the workload and costs of the various projects to have been underestimated.
The recommendation is to completely revise SEM's planning. In its response, the Secretariat assures that it has already initiated the necessary review, so that it can proceed with the work as soon as the decision on the Switzerland-EU package is adopted. The source therefore documents an internal review that has begun and a decision-making step that is still necessary, but does not indicate when the decision will be adopted, what additional resources will be allocated, or what timetable the work will follow.
